title: Scarcity

content.outcome: Explain scarcity and identify tradeoffs created by limited resources
content.core: Scarcity means people, businesses, and governments have limited resources but unlimited wants. Because resources such as time, money, labor, and raw materials are limited, choices must be made. Every choice involves a tradeoff, and those tradeoffs force individuals and societies to decide how to use scarce resources. Scarcity is the basic problem that economics studies.
recognition: Resources are limited, but wants are greater than what can be produced.
A choice must be made between competing uses.
Getting more of one thing means giving up something else.
The question focuses on limits, tradeoffs, or unmet wants.
content.watch: Scarcity does not mean there is almost none of a good. It means the good is limited relative to wants. Even time and money are scarce because they have alternative uses.
content.worked: A student has two hours before an exam and must choose between studying economics or finishing a history paper. The student cannot fully do both. This is scarcity because time is limited, so choosing one use means giving up the other.
content.check: A city has enough money to build either a new park or repair several roads, but not both this year. Why is this an example of scarcity?

title: Incentives

content.outcome: Predict behavioral responses and unintended consequences created by incentives.
content.core: Incentives change the expected benefits or costs of a choice, so they can alter behavior at the margin. The fee alters the next trip's marginal cost, which can change the decision. With limited time, the higher wage makes study more costly in forgone earnings. People respond to incentives, but they may respond in ways that improve the metric while hurting the real goal. The toll raises the cost of using the road, which gives drivers an incentive to change behavior.
recognition: A speed bonus makes workers finish faster, but quality falls.
A new toll reduces traffic on a busy road.
A toll is added to a crowded bridge, and some drivers switch routes.
A school rewards high test pass rates.
An incentive changes the payoff to a choice; it need not be monetary or guarantee a result.
content.watch: A common mistake is to define incentives as cash payments or guaranteed behavior. An incentive changes the expected payoff to a choice; it may be monetary or nonmonetary, and people can respond differently.
content.worked: A city charges a $4 congestion fee for downtown trips during rush hour. A driver whose next trip provides only $3 of benefit will now avoid that trip because its marginal cost has risen by $4. A commuter whose trip is worth $10 will still travel. The fee changes behavior at the margin without guaranteeing that every driver responds in the same way.
content.check: A neighborhood app awards a visible badge for weekly recycling. Participation rises among users who value recognition but barely changes for others. What is the best interpretation?

title: Opportunity Cost

content.outcome: Identify and calculate the value of the next-best alternative.
content.core: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative given up when a choice is made. Scarcity makes opportunity cost unavoidable because using time, money, or resources for one purpose prevents their use elsewhere. The cost is the single best forgone option, valued from the decision maker's perspective, and it can be monetary or nonmonetary.
recognition: Look for a choice between two or more alternatives under a time, money, or resource constraint.
Identify the next-best alternative that the decision maker gives up.
Value the forgone alternative from the decision maker's perspective.
Do not add every rejected option; opportunity cost is the single best alternative forgone.
content.watch: A common mistake is to add the value of every forgone option. Opportunity cost is the value of the single next-best alternative, not the sum of all alternatives.
content.worked: A student can spend Saturday working for $80, studying for an exam worth an estimated $60 benefit, or attending a concert valued at $40. If the student studies, the best forgone alternative is the $80 work shift. The opportunity cost of studying is therefore $80, not $120 and not the concert's $40 value.
content.check: Why can spending an hour in a free park have an opportunity cost?

title: Marginal Analysis

content.outcome: Use marginal benefits and costs while avoiding sunk-cost reasoning.
content.core: Marginal analysis compares the additional benefit of the next unit or small change with its additional cost. A decision should expand while marginal benefit is at least marginal cost and stop before the next unit costs more than it adds. Sunk costs do not affect this forward-looking comparison, while costs or benefits imposed on others matter in social marginal analysis.
recognition: Look for a decision about one more unit, one more hour, or a small change in an activity.
Compare the additional benefit of that change with its additional cost.
Continue while marginal benefit is at least marginal cost; stop before the next unit costs more than it adds.
Ignore totals or averages when the question asks whether the next unit is worthwhile.
content.watch: A common mistake is to decide from total benefit or total cost. Marginal analysis compares the additional benefit and additional cost of the next unit.
content.worked: A warehouse earns $15 from handling one additional box, and the marginal cost of that box is $13. Marginal net benefit is $15 - $13 = $2, so handling the box increases profit. If the next box cost $17 instead, its marginal net benefit would be -$2 and the warehouse should stop before that box.
content.check: Total cost is $100 for 10 units, and producing an eleventh unit adds $15. Which number is average cost, and which is marginal cost?

title: Microeconomics vs. Macroeconomics

content.outcome: Distinguish microeconomic and macroeconomic questions.
content.core: Microeconomics studies choices by individual households, firms, workers, and markets, while macroeconomics studies economy-wide outcomes such as output, inflation, and unemployment. One event can require both market-level and economy-wide analysis. Macro conclusions require appropriate aggregation across people, firms, and markets. Macroeconomics examines economy-wide aggregates such as output, inflation, and unemployment. A single firm's hiring decision is microeconomics.
recognition: A report tracks national inflation, unemployment, and total output.
A firm decides how much labor to hire at one restaurant.
Microeconomics can use massive data while focusing on individual choices and specific markets.
A bakery studies how customers respond to a muffin price increase.
Microeconomics studies choices by households, firms, and specific markets.
content.watch: A common mistake is to label any large organization as macroeconomic. The classification depends on the unit of analysis: one decision-maker is micro; economy-wide aggregates are macro.
content.worked: A restaurant deciding whether to hire one more server is a microeconomic question because it concerns one firm's choice. The national unemployment rate is a macroeconomic outcome because it aggregates labor-market conditions across the economy. The subject's size is not decisive; the unit of analysis is.
content.check: Name three economy-wide outcomes studied in macroeconomics.

title: Positive vs. Normative Analysis

content.outcome: Distinguish testable claims from value judgments.
content.core: Positive analysis makes claims that evidence can test, while normative analysis applies value judgments about what should be done. Identify what observation could support or contradict a testable claim. A positive claim can be false. A normative claim ranks goals or outcomes using values; evidence can inform that judgment but cannot settle the values alone.
recognition: A transit study predicts that a lower fare will increase ridership.
Ridership data can test the prediction even if it turns out to be wrong.
A council member says parks should receive more funding because access is fair.
A commissioner says the city ought to favor safer streets even if travel takes longer.
content.watch: Do not treat positive as good, true, or politically neutral. A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.
content.worked: The statement 'A lower bus fare will increase ridership' is positive because ridership data can support or contradict it. The statement 'The city should lower bus fares because access is fair' is normative because it applies a value judgment. Evidence can inform both statements, but only the first is directly testable as written.
content.check: Is every policy statement normative?

title: Models and Assumptions

content.outcome: Evaluate the purpose, assumptions, simplifications, and limits of economic models.
content.core: Economic models simplify reality to isolate the relationships that matter for a particular question. The two-good abstraction exposes scarcity and opportunity cost without describing every output. Evaluate a model by its purpose, assumptions, performance, and relevant context. Extra complexity is useful only when its benefits exceed lost clarity or robustness. Apply a model where its important assumptions remain reasonable.
recognition: Adding dozens of variables improves historical fit but makes the mechanism impossible to interpret.
A central bank changes its policy rule, and a forecasting relationship estimated under the old rule breaks down.
A local haircut model omits exchange rates and global shipping.
An economist builds a simple two-market circular-flow model and leaves out banks, government, and foreign trade.
An economist studies how price affects purchases while holding income constant.
content.watch: Do not use the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence. Evaluate a model by its purpose, assumptions, performance, and relevant context.
content.worked: A PPF model includes only two goods, even though real economies produce thousands. That simplification isolates scarcity and opportunity cost: moving toward more of one good requires less of the other. The model is useful for that purpose, but it would be inadequate for predicting the output of a specific industry without additional detail.
content.check: What role does an assumption play in a model?

title: Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF)

content.outcome: Interpret PPF points, slopes, shifts, efficiency, growth, and opportunity cost.
content.core: A production possibilities frontier shows the combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its current resources and technology. A bowed-out PPF shows increasing opportunity cost as resources are shifted toward one good. Opportunity cost rises because resources are specialized and become less well suited as they are shifted into the other good. A PPF shows possible production combinations given current resources and technology.
recognition: A PPF shows possible production combinations given current resources and technology.
A new technology improves only medical production.
An economy first removes unemployment, then gains new machinery.
Using idle resources changes the production point; resources or technology shift the frontier.
content.watch: Do not confuse a PPF with a market curve. A PPF shows possible production combinations given current resources and technology. Using idle resources changes the production point; resources or technology shift the frontier.
content.worked: On the PPF, moving from point C (15 units of X and 35 of Y) to point D (21 of X and 20 of Y) gains 6 units of X but gives up 15 units of Y. The total opportunity cost is 15 units of Y, or 15/6 = 2.5 units of Y per additional unit of X.
content.check: Does moving along a PPF represent economic growth?

title: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade

content.outcome: Analyze Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade.
content.core: Comparative advantage belongs to the producer with the lower opportunity cost, even when another producer has an absolute advantage in both goods. Compute the forgone alternative per unit, then select the lower opportunity cost. Specialization creates potential output gains; the trading terms determine whether both sides gain. Use opportunity cost and net benefits to evaluate specialization and exchange. Different opportunity costs create room for specialization and mutually beneficial exchange.
recognition: Use opportunity cost and net benefits to evaluate specialization and exchange.
Different opportunity costs create room for specialization and mutually beneficial exchange.
One lamp costs Ari 2 rugs and costs Bea 6 rugs.
One producer is more productive in both goods.
Two firms specialize and create 40 extra units of combined output.
content.watch: A common mistake is to choose the producer with the greatest absolute output. Comparative advantage depends on lower opportunity cost, and a mutually beneficial terms-of-trade ratio lies between the two opportunity costs.
content.worked: Ari can produce either 12 lamps or 24 rugs, so one lamp costs Ari 24/12 = 2 rugs. Bea can produce either 10 lamps or 60 rugs, so one lamp costs Bea 60/10 = 6 rugs. Ari has comparative advantage in lamps because 2 rugs is the lower opportunity cost; Bea has comparative advantage in rugs because one rug costs Bea 10/60 = 1/6 lamp, below Ari's 12/24 = 1/2 lamp. Specialization according to those lower opportunity costs can increase combined output.
content.check: If 1 X costs 2 Y, what is the cost of 1 Y?

title: Economists and Policy

content.outcome: Analyze the economist's role in policy advice.
content.core: Economists use evidence and models to estimate policy effects, identify tradeoffs, and explain uncertainty. Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences. Economic analysis clarifies tradeoffs but does not uniquely rank every social goal. Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments. Economists analyze incentives, evidence, and tradeoffs; elected officials make policy choices.
recognition: An economist estimates a policy’s effects, then recommends adoption.
Economists analyze incentives, evidence, and tradeoffs; elected officials make policy choices.
Policy evaluation requires explicit objectives and evidence about consequences.
A policy model predicts large benefits, but the data come from a different population and period.
Good advice makes assumptions, tradeoffs, and uncertainty visible.
content.watch: A common mistake is to give economists authority to choose society's values. Economists can estimate consequences and tradeoffs; the policy choice also requires normative judgments.
content.worked: An economist estimates that a proposed transit subsidy will increase ridership by 8%, but the estimate comes from a city with denser development. Professional advice reports the predicted benefit, explains the uncertain transfer to the local setting, and identifies fiscal costs. Whether those consequences justify the policy also depends on public values and priorities.

title: Competitive Markets

content.outcome: Identify the conditions that create price-taking behavior and limited market power
content.core: A competitive market contains many independent buyers and sellers, usually trading products that buyers view as close substitutes. No single participant controls enough of the market to set the market price. A small firm is therefore a price taker: it chooses how much to sell at the price created by market supply and demand. Competition becomes stronger when firms can enter or exit, buyers can compare offers, and switching among sellers is easy.
recognition: Many independent firms sell the same product or close substitutes.
One seller supplies only a small share of total market output.
A firm accepts a price determined by overall market supply and demand.
Buyers can compare prices and switch sellers without much difficulty.
Entry by new firms or exit by existing firms changes competitive pressure.
content.watch: A market is not strictly competitive just because it has several sellers. Product differentiation, search costs, network effects, or barriers to entry can still give firms pricing power. The key question is whether one seller can raise its price persistently without losing many customers to available alternatives.
content.worked: A wheat farmer is one of thousands selling a standardized crop. The posted market price is $6 per bushel. If this farmer asks $7 while other farmers still charge $6, buyers can purchase identical wheat elsewhere. The farmer is too small to move the market price, so raising the price would sharply reduce sales. The evidence - many sellers, a standardized product, and easy switching - identifies price-taking behavior.
content.check: An online marketplace makes prices easy to compare, but a merger leaves one company controlling most available inventory. Which fact strengthens competition, which fact weakens it, and why?

title: Demand & the Law of Demand

content.outcome: Explain demand, quantity demanded, and movements along a demand curve.
content.core: Demand describes the quantities buyers are willing and able to purchase at different prices, holding other demand conditions constant. Quantity demanded is the amount buyers choose at one particular price. The law of demand states that a lower own price increases quantity demanded and a higher own price decreases it, all else equal. An own-price change causes movement between points on the same demand curve; it does not shift the curve.
recognition: The good's own price changes while income, tastes, expectations, related-good prices, and the number of buyers remain constant.
The question asks for quantity demanded at a particular price.
Two points lie on the same downward-sloping demand curve.
A lower price is paired with a larger quantity demanded.
content.watch: A common mistake is to call every change in quantity a shift in demand. If the good's own price changes and buyers move from one point to another on the same demand curve, quantity demanded changes. Demand itself shifts only when a nonprice determinant changes.
content.worked: On the gourmet-donut graph, point A shows a price of $10 and quantity demanded of 100 thousand. Point B shows a lower price of $5 and quantity demanded of 225 thousand. Because both points lie on the same demand curve and only the good's own price changes, the move from A to B is an increase in quantity demanded of 125 thousand, not an increase in demand.
content.check: The price of a concert ticket falls and buyers move to another point on the same demand curve. What changes: demand or quantity demanded?

title: Determinants of Demand

content.outcome: Identify nonprice determinants that shift demand left or right.
content.core: Demand shifts when a nonprice determinant changes. Demand increases and shifts right when buyers want more at every price; demand decreases and shifts left when they want less at every price. Important determinants include income, tastes and preferences, expectations, the number of buyers, and the prices of substitutes and complements. The direction of an income effect depends on whether the good is normal or inferior, and the effect of a related-good price depends on whether the goods are substitutes or complements.
recognition: Consumer income, preferences, expectations, or the number of buyers changes.
The price of a substitute or complement changes.
Quantity demanded changes at the same price.
The entire demand curve moves left or right rather than moving to another point on one curve.
content.watch: Do not treat a change in the good's own price as a demand shifter. Own-price changes create movements along the existing curve. A nonprice determinant changes how much buyers want at every price and shifts the entire curve.
content.worked: At a coffee price of $10, the original curve D0 shows quantity demanded of 50 thousand, while D1 shows 125 thousand. The price of coffee is held constant, so the 75-thousand increase cannot be a movement along D0. It is a rightward shift from D0 to D1, meaning a nonprice determinant has increased demand.
content.check: Income rises for buyers of a normal good. Which direction does its demand curve shift, and why?

title: Supply & the Law of Supply

content.outcome: Explain supply, quantity supplied, and movements along a supply curve.
content.core: Supply describes the quantities sellers are willing and able to offer at different prices, holding other supply conditions constant. Quantity supplied is the amount sellers offer at one particular price. The law of supply states that a higher own price generally increases quantity supplied and a lower own price decreases it, all else equal. An own-price change causes movement between points on the same supply curve; it does not shift the curve.
recognition: The good's own price changes while production conditions remain constant.
The question asks for quantity supplied at a particular price.
Two points lie on the same upward-sloping supply curve.
A higher price is paired with a larger quantity supplied.
content.watch: A common mistake is to call every change in quantity a shift in supply. If the good's own price changes and sellers move from one point to another on the same supply curve, quantity supplied changes. Supply itself shifts only when a nonprice determinant changes.
content.worked: On the coffee supply graph, point A shows a price of $6 and quantity supplied of 100 thousand. Point B shows a higher price of $11 and quantity supplied of 225 thousand. Because both points lie on the same supply curve and only coffee's own price changes, the move from A to B is an increase in quantity supplied of 125 thousand, not an increase in supply.
content.check: The market price of handmade tables rises and sellers move to another point on the same supply curve. What changes?

title: Determinants of Supply

content.outcome: Identify nonprice determinants that shift supply left or right.
content.core: Supply shifts when a nonprice determinant changes. Supply increases and shifts right when sellers can provide more at every price; supply decreases and shifts left when they provide less at every price. Important determinants include input and resource costs, technology and productivity, taxes and subsidies, expectations, the number of sellers, and natural or regulatory production conditions. A change that lowers marginal production cost generally increases supply, while a change that raises marginal cost generally decreases it.
recognition: Input prices, technology, productivity, taxes, or subsidies change.
Producers' expectations or the number of sellers changes.
Quantity supplied changes at the same price.
The entire supply curve moves left or right rather than moving to another point on one curve.
content.watch: Do not treat a change in the good's own price as a supply shifter. Own-price changes create movements along the existing curve. A change in production cost, technology, expectations, or the number of sellers changes how much firms offer at every price and shifts the curve.
content.worked: At a hamburger price of $9, the original curve S0 shows quantity supplied of 200 thousand, while S1 shows 100 thousand. The product's price is unchanged, so the 100-thousand decrease is not a movement along S0. It is a leftward shift from S0 to S1, consistent with a determinant such as higher input costs reducing supply.
content.check: A new technology lowers the cost of producing solar panels. Which direction does supply shift, and why?

title: Market Equilibrium

content.outcome: Determine equilibrium, shortages, surpluses, adjustment, and comparative statics.
content.core: Market equilibrium occurs where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. At that price, buyers can purchase the amount they want and sellers can sell the amount they offer, so there is no pressure for price to change. A demand or supply shift creates a new intersection and can change both equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity.
recognition: Find the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
On a graph, use the intersection of the demand and supply curves.
A price below equilibrium creates a shortage; a price above equilibrium creates a surplus.
Report both the equilibrium price and the corresponding equilibrium quantity.
content.watch: A common mistake is to call any intersection or stated price an equilibrium. Equilibrium occurs only where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
content.worked: On the graph, the new demand and supply curves intersect at a price of $5 and quantity of 150 thousand. The intersection is the only point at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, so it is the new market equilibrium. A price above $5 would create a surplus, while a price below $5 would create a shortage.
content.check: Holding supply constant, which equilibrium outcome follows from an increase in demand?

title: Shortages and Surpluses

content.outcome: Determine equilibrium, shortages, surpluses, adjustment, and comparative statics.
content.core: A shortage occurs when quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied; a surplus occurs when quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded. A surplus occurs when quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded. A shortage occurs when quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied. Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, so there is a shortage. Shortages push price upward. A price above equilibrium creates a surplus because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.
recognition: At the current price, buyers want 180 units and sellers offer 120 units.
A price above equilibrium creates a surplus because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.
A price below equilibrium creates a shortage because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.
A surplus exists when quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded.
content.watch: A common mistake is to reverse shortage and price pressure. Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, so there is a shortage. Shortages push price upward.
content.worked: At a price of $2 per gallon, the graph shows quantity demanded of 200 thousand gallons and quantity supplied of 100 thousand. Because buyers want 100 thousand more gallons than sellers offer, the market has a shortage of 200 - 100 = 100 thousand gallons. Upward pressure on price follows.
content.check: At the current price, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied. What market condition exists?

title: Simultaneous Shifts

content.outcome: Determine equilibrium, shortages, surpluses, adjustment, and comparative statics.
content.core: When demand and supply shift at the same time, each shift contributes separately to the new equilibrium. Analyze how each change affects price and quantity, then combine the directional effects. If both shifts push one variable in the same direction, that result is determinate; if they push in opposite directions, the result depends on the relative size of the shifts.
recognition: Both a demand determinant and a supply determinant change.
A bicycle endorsement raises demand while higher input costs reduce supply.
Analyze each shift separately before combining its price and quantity effects.
Opposing effects on one variable leave its direction ambiguous unless relative shift sizes are known.
content.watch: Do not assume an unchanged price means the market experienced no shifts. A demand increase raises price and quantity, while a supply increase lowers price and raises quantity. Equal price effects can cancel while quantity rises.
content.worked: The original curves D0 and S0 intersect at a price of $3 and quantity of 150 thousand. After demand shifts right to D1 and supply shifts left to S1, the new intersection is $5 and the same quantity of 150 thousand. Both shifts raise price; their opposing quantity effects happen to offset in this graph, though quantity would otherwise be ambiguous.
content.check: Which pair of market changes is shown when the graph moves from D0/S0 to D1/S1?

title: Price Ceilings

content.outcome: Distinguish binding and nonbinding ceilings and analyze shortages and rationing.
content.core: A price ceiling sets a legal maximum price and is binding only when it lies below the market equilibrium price. A binding ceiling keeps price from rising to equilibrium, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied and a shortage develops. A ceiling at or above equilibrium is nonbinding because the market can still reach its equilibrium price.
recognition: Compare the legal maximum price with the market equilibrium price.
A ceiling below equilibrium is binding and creates excess demand.
At the ceiling price, read quantity demanded and quantity supplied; their difference is the shortage.
A ceiling at or above equilibrium is nonbinding and does not change the market outcome.
content.watch: A common mistake is to assume that every price ceiling is binding. A price ceiling above equilibrium is not binding. Since $40 is above the $30 equilibrium price, it does not affect the market.
content.worked: The market equilibrium is $30 and 200 units. A binding ceiling of $20 holds price below equilibrium; buyers demand 250 units while sellers supply 150. The resulting shortage is 250 - 150 = 100 units, so some willing buyers cannot purchase at the controlled price.
content.check: At a binding price ceiling, Qd = 90 and Qs = 60. What is the shortage?

title: Price Floors

content.outcome: Distinguish binding and nonbinding floors and analyze surpluses and unintended effects.
content.core: A price floor sets a legal minimum price and is binding only when it lies above the market equilibrium price. A binding floor keeps price from falling to equilibrium, so quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded and a surplus develops. A floor at or below equilibrium is nonbinding because the market can still reach its equilibrium price.
recognition: Compare the legal minimum price with the market equilibrium price.
A floor above equilibrium is binding and creates excess supply.
At the floor price, read quantity supplied and quantity demanded; their difference is the surplus.
A floor at or below equilibrium is nonbinding and does not change the market outcome.
content.watch: A common mistake is to assume that every price floor is binding. Equilibrium is $30. A floor at $20 is below equilibrium, so it does not prevent the market from reaching $30.
content.worked: The market equilibrium is $30 and 200 units. A binding floor of $40 holds price above equilibrium; sellers offer 250 units while buyers demand 150. The resulting surplus is 250 - 150 = 100 units, so some output remains unsold at the controlled price.
content.check: At a binding price floor, Qs = 110 and Qd = 80. What is the surplus?

pdfText: GENERAL ECONOMICS GEN-ECON-20 Time: 5 minutes Outcome: Distinguish binding and nonbinding floors and analyze surpluses and unintended effects. title: Tax Incidence without Elasticity

content.outcome: Distinguish legal tax assignment from economic burden.
content.core: A tax creates a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive. Legal assignment does not determine who bears the economic burden. Equivalent taxes on buyers or sellers create the same wedge and market outcome. Tax burden depends on market responses, not just who is legally assigned to pay.
recognition: Look for a per-unit tax that separates the price buyers pay from the price sellers receive.
Find the new quantity where the vertical gap between demand and supply equals the tax.
The buyer burden is the rise in the buyer price; the seller burden is the fall in the seller price.
Do not infer burden from who sends the tax payment to the government.
content.watch: A common mistake is to assume that legal tax assignment determines the full economic burden. Tax burden depends on market responses, not just who is legally assigned to pay.

title: Tax Incidence with Elasticity

content.outcome: Use elasticity to determine and calculate the distribution of tax burdens.
content.core: Tax incidence depends on relative elasticity: the less responsive side of the market bears more of the tax burden. That side changes quantity less when the tax alters the price it pays or receives, so more of the tax wedge appears on its side of the market. Legal responsibility for remitting the tax does not determine its economic burden.
recognition: The more elastic side can respond more easily, so it bears less of the tax burden.
The less elastic side bears more of the tax burden; identify that side from the market conditions.
A tax on cigarettes causes only a small drop in quantity but a large increase in buyer price.
In one market, demand is much more elastic than supply.
content.watch: A common mistake is to assume that the more elastic side bears more of a tax. The less elastic side bears more. In this particular worked graph, the price changes show an equal split; do not assume buyers always bear more.
content.worked: The untaxed equilibrium price is $15. With the tax, buyers pay $18, sellers receive $12, and 80 units are sold. Buyers bear $18 - $15 = $3 per unit, so their total burden is $3 x 80 = $240. Sellers bear the remaining $3 per unit.
content.check: When demand is less elastic than supply, which side is less able to avoid the tax?

title: International Trade: World Prices

content.outcome: Interpret International Trade: World Prices.
content.core: A world price lets a small country trade at a price determined outside its domestic market. When the world price is below the domestic no-trade equilibrium price, domestic buyers demand more than domestic firms supply and the country imports the difference. When the world price is above the no-trade price, domestic firms supply more than buyers demand and the country exports the difference. Trade changes domestic production, consumption, and the distribution of surplus.
recognition: Compare the world price with the domestic no-trade equilibrium price.
A world price below the no-trade price makes the country an importer.
A world price above the no-trade price makes the country an exporter.
At the world price, imports equal domestic quantity demanded minus quantity supplied; exports use the reverse difference.
content.watch: Do not use high demand instead of world price comparison. A lower world price creates excess domestic demand that is filled by imports.
content.worked: The domestic no-trade equilibrium price is $7. When the country opens to free trade at a world price of $5, domestic buyers demand more than domestic firms supply, and imports fill the difference. Because the world price is below the no-trade price, the country is an importer of this good.
content.check: A student says abundant domestic supply automatically makes a country an exporter. What is missing?

title: International Trade: Tariffs

content.outcome: Analyze International Trade: Tariffs.
content.core: A tariff is a tax on imported goods that raises the domestic price above the world price. Domestic firms respond by producing more, consumers buy less, and imports fall. Consumers lose surplus, domestic producers gain surplus, and the government collects tariff revenue. The tariff also prevents mutually beneficial trades, creating deadweight loss from excessive domestic production and reduced consumption.
recognition: Begin with an importing country whose world price is below the domestic no-trade price.
Add the tariff per unit to the world price to find the tariff-inclusive domestic price.
At that higher price, read domestic quantity demanded and quantity supplied; imports equal their difference.
Tariff revenue equals the tariff per unit multiplied by the number of units imported.
Look for lower consumer surplus, higher producer surplus, government revenue, and deadweight loss from overproduction and underconsumption.
content.watch: Do not treat tariff revenue as full welfare loss. Part of the consumer loss is transferred to producers and government; the production and consumption distortions are net losses.
content.worked: At the $4 world price, domestic quantity demanded is 250 thousand and domestic quantity supplied is 50 thousand, so free-trade imports are 200 thousand. A $2 tariff raises the domestic price to $6; quantity demanded falls to 200 thousand and quantity supplied rises to 100 thousand. Imports fall to 100 thousand, and government tariff revenue is $2 x 100 thousand = $200 thousand.
content.check: Which two effects create tariff deadweight loss?

title: International Trade: Quotas

content.outcome: Analyze International Trade: Quotas.
content.core: An import quota directly limits the quantity of a good that may enter the country. A binding quota reduces imports below their free-trade level, raises the domestic price, increases domestic production, and reduces domestic consumption. The price gap between the domestic quota price and the world price creates quota rent. Who receives that rent affects the country's national-surplus result, while the production and consumption distortions create deadweight loss.
recognition: Begin with the free-trade outcome at the world price.
A binding import quota limits imports below their free-trade quantity.
The restriction raises domestic price, increases domestic production, and reduces domestic consumption.
The gap between the quota price and world price creates quota rent on each permitted import.
Look for deadweight loss from excessive domestic production and reduced consumption.
content.watch: Do not assume quota rent automatically becomes government revenue. It accrues to whoever holds the import rights; auctioning those rights can transfer the rent to government. The recipient matters for national welfare, while production and consumption distortions create deadweight loss.
content.worked: Before trade, domestic supply and demand intersect at a price of $7. With free trade, buyers can purchase at the $3 world price, which creates imports. The quota limits imports, so the domestic price rises to $6. The difference between the $6 quota price and the $3 world price is $3 per imported unit; that $3 gap is quota rent.
content.check: A student says equivalent tariffs and quotas remain identical after demand changes. What is the key difference?

title: International Trade: Policy and Distribution

content.outcome: Evaluate International Trade: Policy and Distribution.
content.core: Trade protection redistributes income and usually reduces total surplus, so a policy claim must be evaluated against its costs and alternatives. Security, infant-industry, employment, and bargaining arguments may identify legitimate goals, but each claim requires evidence that the policy can achieve the goal and that a less costly policy is unavailable. Sound analysis separates measurable economic effects from the value judgments used to choose among them.
recognition: Security can be legitimate, but the claim still requires evidence and comparison.
Compare the free-trade and quota outcomes.
An infant-industry argument requires a temporary, evidence-based learning mechanism and net benefits.
Efficiency concerns total surplus; equity concerns distribution.
Adjustment goals can be pursued through policies with different efficiency costs.
content.watch: Do not ignore efficiency or distribution evidence. Security can be legitimate, but the claim still requires evidence and comparison. An infant-industry argument requires a temporary, evidence-based learning mechanism and net benefits.
content.worked: Suppose protection preserves 1,000 domestic jobs but costs consumers $30 million each year. The positive analysis reports both effects and asks whether less costly policies could assist affected workers. The normative decision then weighs security, distribution, and adjustment goals against the efficiency cost. Saying only that protection 'saves jobs' leaves the consumer cost and alternatives unexamined.
content.check: What is missing from the claim “protection saves jobs”?

title: Price Signals

content.outcome: Explain how prices coordinate buyers, sellers, and resource allocation.
content.core: Prices coordinate decentralized decisions by communicating scarcity and changing the incentives facing buyers and sellers. Information about waiting costs can redirect users much like a price signal. A higher price raises the cost of consuming the good and encourages substitution or conservation. A higher price communicates stronger scarcity or demand pressure and encourages supply responses. A supply improvement can lower price by reducing the good’s relative scarcity.
recognition: A higher price communicates stronger scarcity or demand pressure and encourages supply responses.
The price of a product falls after a new production technology spreads.
A congested road has no toll.
A price rises while quantity sold also rises.
A shortage persists because a legal ceiling prevents price from rising.
content.watch: A common mistake is to assume that a higher price always tells buyers and sellers to do the same thing. It discourages quantity demanded while encouraging quantity supplied, coordinating opposite responses.
content.worked: A hospital posts current wait times of 90 minutes at Clinic A and 20 minutes at Clinic B. Patients who can use either location shift toward Clinic B. The posted wait acts like a nonmoney price signal: it communicates relative congestion and reallocates demand without changing the medical fee.
content.check: What response does a higher market price normally encourage from sellers?

title: Tax Wedges and Revenue

content.outcome: Calculate tax wedges, buyer and seller prices, quantity effects, and revenue.
content.core: A per-unit tax creates a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive. The wedge reduces the quantity traded because some exchanges whose benefits formerly exceeded their costs no longer occur. Tax revenue equals the per-unit wedge multiplied by the post-tax quantity, while the lost mutually beneficial trades create deadweight loss.
recognition: Identify the tax wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive.
Use the post-tax quantity, not the original equilibrium quantity, when measuring revenue.
Tax revenue equals the per-unit tax multiplied by the quantity traded after the tax.
A tax normally reduces quantity traded and creates deadweight loss from forgone exchanges.
content.watch: Do not use pre tax quantity or buyer price change only. The tax is $46 - $34 = $12. Tax revenue is $12 × 420 = $5,040.
content.worked: The untaxed equilibrium is $15 at 100 units. After the tax, buyers pay $18, sellers receive $12, and quantity falls to 80. The tax wedge is $18 - $12 = $6 per unit, so government revenue is $6 x 80 = $480.

title: Market Failures

content.outcome: Identify externalities, public goods, market power, and corrective policy logic.
content.core: A market failure occurs when private decisions do not produce an efficient allocation of resources. An externality affects people outside the transaction. Public goods are nonrival and nonexcludable; common resources are rival and hard to exclude. Identify the wedge between private incentives and social value or cost. Public goods are characterized by nonrivalry and nonexcludability.
recognition: Identify the wedge between private incentives and social value or cost.
Public goods are characterized by nonrivalry and nonexcludability.
A storm-warning signal can serve another listener without reducing its value and nonpayers are hard to exclude.
Public goods are nonrival and nonexcludable; common resources are rival and hard to exclude.
A seller can profitably influence price by restricting output.
content.watch: Do not confuse government provision with the economic definition of a public good. Public goods are characterized by nonrivalry and nonexcludability. Identify the wedge between private incentives and social value or cost.
content.worked: A factory's production imposes $8 of pollution damage per unit on nearby residents, but the factory pays only its $20 private marginal cost. Social marginal cost is $20 + $8 = $28. If buyers' marginal benefit is $24, the unit looks worthwhile privately but destroys $4 of social surplus, demonstrating an external-cost market failure.
content.check: What makes an effect an externality?

title: Price Elasticity of Demand

content.outcome: Calculate midpoint price elasticity of demand and interpret the result
content.core: Price elasticity of demand measures how strongly quantity demanded responds to a price change: PED = absolute percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price. The midpoint method uses the average of the two quantities and the average of the two prices, so reversing the direction gives the same result. Demand is elastic when PED is greater than 1, unit elastic at 1, and inelastic below 1. Elasticity uses percentages, not raw unit changes or visual slope. Close substitutes, a longer adjustment period, a larger budget share, and a narrower market definition generally make demand more elastic.
recognition: Two price-quantity points are provided for a midpoint calculation.
The problem asks whether the quantity response is elastic, unit elastic, or inelastic.
Substitutes, time to adjust, budget share, or market scope are changing.
A linear demand curve has constant slope but different elasticity along the line.
A horizontal or vertical demand curve represents a limiting elasticity case.
content.watch: A steeper-looking curve is not automatically less elastic. Slope uses the original price and quantity units, while elasticity compares percentage changes and depends on the price-quantity location. Put percentage quantity change in the numerator, use midpoint averages in both denominators, and classify demand using the absolute value of PED.
content.worked: Between C and B, price falls from $12 to $8 while quantity demanded rises from 30 to 60. Using midpoint values, quantity changes by 66.7% and price changes by 40.0%, so PED = 66.7% / 40.0% = 1.67. Because 1.67 is greater than 1, demand is elastic over this interval: quantity responds proportionally more than price changes.
content.check: Using points B (P = $8, Q = 60) and A (P = $4, Q = 90), what is midpoint PED, and how should demand be classified over that interval?

title: Price Elasticity of Supply

content.outcome: Measure Price Elasticity of Supply.
content.core: Price elasticity of supply measures the percentage response of quantity supplied to a one-percent change in price. Price Elasticity of Supply measures and interprets how quantity supplied responds to price changes, including time horizon, capacity, storage, determinants, and midpoint calculations. Storage creates another margin through which sellers can respond to price changes. Investment and capacity adjustment make long-run supply more responsive. Price elasticity of supply compares the percentage change in quantity supplied with the percentage change in the good’s price.
recognition: Look for a percentage change in quantity supplied caused by a percentage change in the good's price.
Compute elasticity as percentage change in quantity supplied divided by percentage change in price.
A larger elasticity means sellers respond more strongly to the price change.
Supply is usually more elastic when firms have more time or spare capacity to adjust production.
content.watch: Do not confuse supply elasticity with demand shifters. Price elasticity of supply compares the percentage change in quantity supplied with the percentage change in the good’s price.
content.worked: The price rises from $4 to $8. On the short-run curve, quantity rises from 60 to 70, so the midpoint quantity change is 10/65 = 15.4%; the midpoint price change is 4/6 = 66.7%. Short-run supply elasticity is 15.4%/66.7% = 0.23, which is inelastic. The flatter long-run curve shows a larger quantity response.
content.check: Using the midpoint method, the price of artisan bread loaves changes from $4 to $5 and quantity supplied changes from 900 to 1080. What is price elasticity of supply?

title: Income Elasticity of Demand

content.outcome: Calculate Income Elasticity of Demand.
content.core: Income elasticity of demand measures how demand changes when consumer income changes. Income elasticity helps firms anticipate demand shifts as consumer income changes. Different income responses shift the composition of demand as purchasing power changes. Normal goods have positive income elasticity because demand moves with income. A small percentage demand response relative to income means an income elasticity near zero.
recognition: Demand for restaurant meals rises when consumer income rises.
A small percentage demand response relative to income means an income elasticity near zero.
Household income rises and demand for bus rides falls.
A retailer estimates income elasticity for its store brand at -0.6.
Demand for a normal good rises as income rises.
content.watch: A common mistake is to misread the sign of income elasticity. A positive coefficient identifies a normal good; a negative coefficient identifies an inferior good.
content.worked: Household income rises by 10%, and demand for restaurant meals rises by 15%. Income elasticity is 15% / 10% = 1.5. The positive sign identifies restaurant meals as a normal good, and the coefficient above 1 indicates that demand responds more than proportionally to income in this example.
content.check: Income changes by 5 percent and demand for premium gym memberships changes by 8 percent. What is income elasticity of demand?

title: Cross-Price Elasticity of Demand

content.outcome: Calculate Cross-Price Elasticity of Demand.
content.core: Cross-price elasticity measures how demand for one good responds to a price change in another good. A large positive cross-price coefficient signals a strong substitution relationship. Complementary goods connect through opposite movements between one price and the other good's demand. Demand for one good moving in the same direction as the other good’s price implies positive cross-price elasticity. Little demand response to the other good’s price implies little economic relationship between the goods.
recognition: The price of butter rises and demand for margarine rises.
Little demand response to the other good’s price implies little economic relationship between the goods.
Cross-price elasticity between printers and ink cartridges is -0.7.
A negative cross-price coefficient means demand moves opposite the other good’s price.
The price of Product Y falls 8 percent.
content.watch: Do not confuse cross price with income or own price. A negative cross-price elasticity indicates complements, so higher printer prices reduce demand for ink.
content.worked: The price of printers rises by 10%, and demand for ink cartridges falls by 7%. Cross-price elasticity is -7% / 10% = -0.7. The negative sign indicates that printers and ink cartridges are complements because a higher price for printers reduces demand for ink.
content.check: The price of Product Y rises 10 percent. Cross-price elasticity of demand for Product X is −0.5. Demand for X is predicted to:?

title: Elasticity and Total Revenue

content.outcome: Connect Elasticity and Total Revenue.
content.core: Total revenue equals price multiplied by quantity, and the effect of a price change depends on demand elasticity. A point on demand supplies the price and quantity needed to calculate revenue. At unit elasticity the price and quantity percentage effects offset, marking the revenue peak on a standard linear demand curve.
recognition: Calculate total revenue as price multiplied by quantity at each relevant point.
If price and total revenue move in opposite directions, demand is elastic over that range.
If price and total revenue move in the same direction, demand is inelastic over that range.
At unit elasticity, a small price change leaves total revenue approximately unchanged.
content.watch: A common mistake is to compute elasticity without checking the associated total-revenue change. With elastic demand, price and total revenue move in opposite directions; with inelastic demand, they move together.
content.worked: At point C, price is $12 and quantity is 30, so total revenue is $12 x 30 = $360. At point B, price is $8 and quantity is 60, so revenue is $480. Moving from C to B lowers price but raises total revenue by $120, indicating elastic demand over that segment.
content.check: For luxury cruise cabins, price changes from $3200 to $2880 while quantity demanded changes from 1,500 to 1,900. Use the midpoint method and the observed revenue totals. Which statement is correct?

title: Applications of Elasticity

content.outcome: Apply Applications of Elasticity.
content.core: Elasticity helps predict tax incidence, deadweight loss, pricing responses, and other outcomes that depend on how strongly quantity responds. Market power is stronger when buyers have fewer substitutes. Labor demand is a derived factor demand. The less elastic side of the market changes quantity less and bears more of the tax burden. With elastic demand, a price increase can cause a proportionally larger loss of quantity demanded.
recognition: The less elastic side of the market changes quantity less and bears more of the tax burden.
With elastic demand, a price increase can cause a proportionally larger loss of quantity demanded.
More responsive buyers and sellers reduce traded quantity more when a tax wedge is introduced.
A firm estimates demand elasticity at 2.1.
Elastic demand produces a larger percentage quantity response to a given percentage price change.
content.watch: A common mistake is to fail to connect output and input demand. When customers readily reduce output purchases, firms more strongly reduce input use after cost increases.
content.worked: Two sides of a market face a $6 tax. Buyers have few substitutes and reduce purchases only slightly, while sellers can redirect output to other markets. Demand is less elastic than supply, so buyers bear more of the tax through a larger increase in the price they pay.
content.check: If supply is much less elastic than demand, sellers usually bear:?

title: Consumer Surplus & Willingness to Pay

content.outcome: Explain Consumer Surplus & Willingness to Pay.
content.core: Consumer surplus is the difference between a buyer's willingness to pay and the price actually paid. Surplus analysis compares value created with the opportunity cost of the resources used. Demand can be interpreted as buyers' marginal willingness to pay. The gain from an additional trade is the buyer’s willingness to pay minus the seller’s cost, not either side’s individual surplus alone.
recognition: Look for a buyer's willingness to pay and the market price actually paid.
Individual consumer surplus equals willingness to pay minus price.
On a graph, consumer surplus is the area below demand and above the market price up to the quantity traded.
A buyer whose willingness to pay is below price does not purchase and earns no consumer surplus.
content.watch: Do not assume every trade creates surplus. The gain from an additional trade is the buyer’s willingness to pay minus the seller’s cost, not either side’s individual surplus alone.
content.worked: At equilibrium, price is $14 and quantity is 8. The demand intercept of $30 represents the highest willingness to pay. Consumer surplus is the triangle above price and below demand: 1/2 x 8 x ($30 - $14) = $64.
content.check: Why is the rectangle below market price not consumer surplus?

title: Producer Surplus & Willingness to Accept

content.outcome: Explain Producer Surplus & Willingness to Accept.
content.core: Producer surplus is the difference between the price a seller receives and the seller's willingness to accept. Surplus analysis compares value created with the opportunity cost of the resources used. Producer surplus is the price-cost gap across units supplied. Producer surplus measures the price received above the seller’s willingness to accept for that unit.
recognition: Look for a seller's willingness to accept or marginal cost and the price received.
Individual producer surplus equals price received minus willingness to accept.
On a graph, producer surplus is the area above supply and below the market price up to the quantity traded.
A seller whose cost exceeds the market price does not make that trade.
content.watch: Do not confuse wta price gap. Producer surplus measures the price received above the seller’s willingness to accept for that unit.
content.worked: At equilibrium, price is $14 and quantity is 8. The supply intercept is $6, so producer surplus is the triangle above supply and below price: 1/2 x 8 x ($14 - $6) = $32.
content.check: Why is the full area above supply not producer surplus?

title: Total Surplus & Gains from Exchange

content.outcome: Calculate Total Surplus & Gains from Exchange.
content.core: Total surplus equals consumer surplus plus producer surplus and measures the gains created by exchange. Each trade adds to total surplus when the buyer's willingness to pay exceeds the seller's opportunity cost. Total surplus is maximized when every mutually beneficial trade occurs and no trade with a cost above its value is completed.
recognition: Add consumer surplus and producer surplus to obtain total surplus.
For each possible trade, compare the buyer's willingness to pay with the seller's opportunity cost.
A trade creates gains when buyer value exceeds seller cost.
On a graph, total surplus is the area between demand and supply up to the quantity traded.
content.watch: A common mistake is to fail to separate transfer from total loss. Consumer surplus is $10 and producer surplus is $8; their sum equals the $18 gain from exchange.

title: Efficient Quantity & Allocation

content.outcome: Identify Efficient Quantity & Allocation.
content.core: The efficient quantity includes every unit whose buyer value is at least as large as its opportunity cost. Efficiency pairs the highest-value buyers with the lowest-cost sellers and continues exchange while the next buyer's willingness to pay covers the next seller's cost. Producing beyond that point destroys surplus, while stopping before it leaves gains unrealized.
recognition: Order potential trades from the highest buyer value and the lowest seller cost.
Complete every trade for which willingness to pay is at least as large as opportunity cost.
Stop when the next seller's cost exceeds the next buyer's value.
An efficient allocation sends the good to the highest-value buyers and production to the lowest-cost sellers.
content.watch: A common mistake is to equate more output with more efficiency. The forced extra unit contributes $23 - $29 = -$6 to total surplus.
content.worked: Demand and supply intersect at 8 units and $10. At that quantity, the marginal buyer's value equals the marginal seller's cost. Units below 8 create positive gains from trade; units above 8 cost more than buyers value them. The efficient allocation therefore produces 8 units.

title: Changes in Surplus & Policy Effects

content.outcome: Trace Changes in Surplus & Policy Effects.
content.core: A price or policy change can transfer surplus between buyers and sellers and can destroy surplus by preventing mutually beneficial trades. A transfer changes who receives existing gains without changing their total. Deadweight loss is different: it represents gains from exchange that disappear because quantity moves away from the efficient level.
recognition: Establish the initial consumer surplus, producer surplus, and total surplus before the change.
Recalculate those areas after the price change or policy intervention.
Separate transfers between buyers and sellers from surplus that disappears entirely.
Deadweight loss represents mutually beneficial trades prevented by the change.
content.watch: A common mistake is to count only existing buyers or only new buyers. With the same trades still occurring, the price change transfers surplus dollar for dollar from sellers to buyers; it does not change total surplus.

title: Efficiency, Equity & Limits of Surplus Analysis

content.outcome: Distinguish Efficiency, Equity & Limits of Surplus Analysis.
content.core: Efficiency concerns the size of total surplus, while equity concerns how benefits and costs are distributed. The efficiency result is positive analysis; deciding whether the distribution is fair adds a normative criterion. Surplus analysis compares value created with the opportunity cost of the resources used. Observed willingness to pay reflects both preferences and purchasing power. Efficiency and equity are different criteria; maximizing total gains does not determine how those gains are shared.
recognition: Use total surplus to evaluate efficiency and distributional evidence to evaluate equity.
Recognize that the allocation with the largest total surplus need not be the most equal.
Remember that measured willingness to pay depends partly on ability to pay.
A policy judgment requires an explicit value choice when efficiency and equity point in different directions.
content.watch: Do not treat efficiency as equity. Observed willingness to pay reflects both preferences and purchasing power. A has $150 private surplus but $110 after the external cost; B has $140 and no stated external cost.
content.worked: Policy A creates $500 of total surplus divided evenly between buyers and sellers. Policy B creates $520 of total surplus but gives $500 to sellers and $20 to buyers. Policy B is more efficient because total surplus is larger, but whether its distribution is more equitable is a separate normative judgment.
content.check: A student says efficiency requires equal gains. Correction?

title: Domestic Production, Consumption & Trade Quantities

content.outcome: Determine Domestic Production, Consumption & Trade Quantities.
content.core: At a world price, domestic consumption is read from demand and domestic production is read from supply. When domestic consumption exceeds domestic production, imports fill the difference; when production exceeds consumption, the excess is exported. The comparison must be made at the world price because that price guides both domestic buyers and sellers under free trade.
recognition: Compare the world price with the domestic no-trade equilibrium price.
At the world price, read domestic consumption from demand and domestic production from supply.
When consumption exceeds production, imports equal domestic consumption minus domestic production.
When production exceeds consumption, exports equal domestic production minus domestic consumption.
content.watch: A common mistake is to omit one or more welfare components. Revenue is tariff×imports; each side distortion is a triangle. Total DWL is $144.
content.worked: Without trade, domestic supply and demand intersect at $7 and 175 thousand avocados. At the $10 world price, domestic consumers buy 100 thousand while domestic producers supply 250 thousand. The country exports the difference: 250 - 100 = 150 thousand avocados.

title: Gains from Trade, Surplus & Winners/Losers

content.outcome: Calculate Gains from Trade, Surplus & Winners/Losers.
content.core: International trade changes consumer and producer surplus and creates net gains when the world price differs from the no-trade equilibrium price. The surplus framework converts distributional changes into a net total-surplus comparison. Trade creates net gains while redistributing surplus between buyers and sellers.
recognition: Trade creates net gains while redistributing surplus between buyers and sellers.
The efficiency result is based on the net change in combined surplus, not on every group winning.
Higher export prices redistribute surplus toward producers while creating a positive net gain in the standard model.
Aggregate gains do not imply universal gains.
content.watch: Do not assume trade has only winners or only losers. Trade creates net gains while redistributing surplus between buyers and sellers. The efficiency result is based on the net change in combined surplus, not on every group winning.

title: Economic Costs: Explicit, Implicit & Opportunity Cost

content.outcome: Distinguish Economic Costs: Explicit, Implicit & Opportunity Cost.
content.core: Economic cost includes both explicit payments and the implicit opportunity costs of owner-supplied resources. Explicit costs require cash payments to outside suppliers, while implicit costs measure the value of income or returns forgone by using the owner's time, money, or property in the business. Economic decisions count both because every resource has a next-best use.
recognition: Classify cash payments to outside suppliers as explicit costs.
Identify the income or return sacrificed on owner-supplied time, money, or property as an implicit cost.
Economic cost includes both explicit and implicit opportunity costs.
Do not treat an owner-supplied resource as free merely because no check is written.
content.watch: A common mistake is to count only recorded expense. Economic cost equals explicit cost plus all implicit opportunity costs: $70,000 + $40,000 + $5,000.
content.worked: A business pays $70,000 in wages and rent. The owner also gives up a $40,000 salary and $5,000 of interest that invested capital could have earned elsewhere. Explicit cost is $70,000; implicit cost is $45,000; economic cost is $70,000 + $45,000 = $115,000.

title: Accounting, Economic & Normal Profit

content.outcome: Calculate and interpret accounting profit, economic profit, implicit costs, and normal profit.
content.core: Accounting profit subtracts explicit costs from revenue, while economic profit also subtracts implicit opportunity costs. Normal profit is the return required to keep owner-supplied resources in their current use, so it is included among implicit costs. Zero economic profit therefore means the firm covers every explicit and implicit cost, not that the owner receives nothing.
recognition: Start with total revenue and identify both explicit and implicit costs.
Accounting profit subtracts explicit costs only; economic profit subtracts both kinds of cost.
Normal profit is the owner's opportunity cost and is included among implicit costs.
Zero economic profit can coexist with positive accounting profit.
content.watch: Do not treat zero economic profit as failure. Zero economic profit includes normal compensation for owner resources. The $85,000 accounting profit exactly covers the $85,000 of implicit opportunity costs.
content.worked: A firm earns $200,000 of revenue and pays $115,000 of explicit costs, so accounting profit is $85,000. If the owner's forgone salary, interest, and rent also total $85,000, economic profit is $85,000 - $85,000 = $0. The firm still earns normal profit because its resources receive their opportunity-cost return.

title: Cost Components & Cost Schedules

content.outcome: Complete short-run cost schedules using total and average cost identities
content.core: In the short run, total fixed cost (TFC) does not change with output, while total variable cost (TVC) rises or falls as production changes. Total cost combines both components: TC = TFC + TVC. For positive output Q, divide each total by Q: AFC = TFC / Q, AVC = TVC / Q, and ATC = TC / Q = AFC + AVC. At zero output, TVC is normally zero, TC equals TFC, and average costs are undefined because division by zero is impossible. On a total-cost graph, the vertical distance between TC and TVC equals TFC at every quantity.
recognition: A cost-schedule row is missing TFC, TVC, or TC.
A fixed payment remains even when current output is zero.
A cost changes when labor, materials, or production changes.
The vertical gap between TC and TVC is compared across quantities.
Total costs must be converted to per-unit AFC, AVC, or ATC.
content.watch: Do not subtract or multiply fixed and variable cost when finding total cost: add them. Also distinguish total fixed cost from average fixed cost. TFC stays constant as output changes, but AFC = TFC / Q falls as the same fixed amount is spread across more units. Average costs are not defined at Q = 0.
content.worked: At Q = 120, the graph shows total cost of $1,200 and total variable cost of $800. The $400 vertical gap between the two curves is total fixed cost because TC = TFC + TVC. Dividing each cost by 120 gives AFC = $3.33, AVC = $6.67, and ATC = $10.00. As a check, AFC + AVC = ATC.
content.check: At Q = 10, a schedule shows TFC = $90 and TC = $250. What are TVC, AFC, AVC, and ATC, and how can you verify that AFC + AVC = ATC?

pdfText: MICROECONOMICS MICRO-21 Time: 6 minutes Outcome: Complete short-run cost schedules using total and average cost identities Difficulty: Intermediate Cost Components & Cost Schedules THE CORE IDEA In the short run, total fixed cost (TFC) does not change with output, while total variable cost (TVC) rises or falls as production changes. Total cost combines both components: TC = TFC + TVC. For positive output Q, divide each total by Q: AFC = TFC / Q, AVC = TVC / Q, and ATC = TC / Q = AFC + AVC. At zero output, TVC is normally zero, TC equals TFC, and average costs are undefined because division by zero is impossible. On a total-cost graph, the vertical distance between TC and TVC equals TFC at every quantity. HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT • A cost-schedule row is missing TFC, TVC, or TC. • A fixed payment remains even when current output is zero. • A cost changes when labor, materials, or production changes. • The vertical gap between TC and TVC is compared across quantities. • Total costs must be converted to per-unit AFC, AVC, or ATC. WATCH OUT Do not subtract or multiply fixed and variable cost when finding total cost: add them. Also distinguish total fixed cost from average fixed cost. TFC stays constant as output changes, but AFC = TFC / Q falls as the same fixed amount is spread across more units. Average costs are not defined at Q = 0. WORKED EXAMPLE: BUILDING A COST SCHEDULE At Q = 120, the graph shows total cost of $1,200 and total variable cost of $800. The $400 vertical gap between the two curves is total fixed cost because TC = TFC + TVC. Dividing each cost by 120 gives AFC = $3.33, AVC = $6.67, and ATC = $10.00. As a check, AFC + AVC = ATC. CHECK YOURSELF At Q = 10, a schedule shows TFC = $90 and TC = $250. What are TVC, AFC, AVC, and ATC, and how can you verify that AFC + AVC = ATC? READY? Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Average Costs: AFC, AVC & ATC

content.outcome: Calculate Average Costs: AFC, AVC & ATC.
content.core: Average fixed cost, average variable cost, and average total cost express costs per unit of output. Average total cost equals average fixed cost plus average variable cost. Average fixed cost falls as output spreads the same fixed cost across more units, while average variable cost changes with the productivity and price of variable inputs.
recognition: Divide fixed cost by output for average fixed cost and variable cost by output for average variable cost.
Average total cost equals average fixed cost plus average variable cost.
Average fixed cost falls continuously as output spreads the same fixed cost across more units.
Use per-unit measures only when output is positive.
content.watch: A common mistake is to misuse average cost formula. AVC = $300/20 = $15; AFC = $5; ATC = $20. TVC = $1,000; AVC = $20, AFC = $8, and ATC = $28.
content.worked: At 400 units, the graph shows average cost of $20 and average variable cost of $12. Because AC = AVC + AFC, average fixed cost is $20 - $12 = $8 per unit. The gap between AC and AVC is therefore the firm's average fixed cost.

title: Marginal Cost & Production-Cost Linkages

content.outcome: Calculate Marginal Cost & Production-Cost Linkages.
content.core: Marginal cost is the change in total cost caused by producing one more unit. Divide the input cost by marginal product. Higher MP lowers variable input cost per extra unit. A constant addition to cost at every output does not change the cost of producing one more unit.
recognition: Look for the change in total cost caused by producing one additional unit.
Compute marginal cost as the change in total cost divided by the change in output.
A fixed-cost change does not change marginal cost, but a variable-input cost change usually does.
When marginal product falls, marginal cost tends to rise if the input price is unchanged.
content.watch: A common mistake is to move mp and mc together. Higher MP lowers variable input cost per extra unit. A constant addition to cost at every output does not change the cost of producing one more unit.
content.worked: Marginal cost crosses AVC at AVC's minimum of $10 and 200 units, then crosses AC at AC's minimum of $20 and 400 units. When marginal cost is below an average, it pulls that average down; when marginal cost rises above it, the average begins to increase.
content.check: If output rises by 1 unit and total cost rises by $18, marginal cost of that unit is:?

title: Short-Run Cost Curves: Relationships & Shifts

content.outcome: Analyze Short-Run Cost Curves: Relationships & Shifts.
content.core: Short-run cost curves move differently because fixed costs affect AFC and ATC, while variable-input costs affect AVC, ATC, and MC. A below-average marginal observation pulls the average down. Labor is the variable input in the standard short-run model. A fixed-cost increase raises fixed cost per unit and total cost per unit but leaves variable and marginal cost unchanged.
recognition: A fixed-cost increase raises fixed cost per unit and total cost per unit but leaves variable and marginal cost unchanged.
A technology improvement reduces the variable input needed at every output.
Labor is the variable input in the standard short-run model.
A firm receives a property-tax increase that does not depend on output.
content.watch: A common mistake is to mix fixed and variable shifts. A fixed-cost increase raises fixed cost per unit and total cost per unit but leaves variable and marginal cost unchanged.
content.worked: Suppose the firm signs a more expensive lease while output and variable input prices are unchanged. The higher fixed cost raises average fixed cost and therefore shifts ATC upward. AVC and MC remain in the positions shown because neither depends on fixed cost. The production decision at the margin is unchanged.

title: Sunk & Avoidable Costs

content.outcome: Distinguish Sunk & Avoidable Costs.
content.core: Sunk costs cannot be recovered and should not affect a current decision; avoidable costs change with the option chosen. Past unrecoverable costs do not change the marginal consequences of the current decision. The relevant comparison is forward-looking, not an attempt to reverse an unrecoverable past payment. The current payment is sunk; the future renewal is avoidable and differs across options. Avoidable costs differ across the alternatives being considered.
recognition: Ask whether a cost has already been incurred and cannot be recovered.
Exclude sunk costs from the comparison among current options.
Include avoidable costs because they differ depending on which option is chosen.
Focus on future benefits and future costs that change with the decision.
content.watch: Do not treat fixed as sunk. The current payment is sunk; the future renewal is avoidable and differs across options. Avoidable costs differ across the alternatives being considered.
content.worked: A theater has already paid a nonrefundable $4,000 license fee. Canceling tonight's show avoids $3,000 of staffing and utility costs but gives up $5,500 of ticket revenue. The sunk $4,000 does not affect the current decision. Because operating adds $5,500 - $3,000 = $2,500, the theater should hold the show.
content.check: A fixed annual license can be surrendered halfway through the year for a $4,000 refund. For a midyear shutdown decision, which amount is relevant?

title: LRAC, Economies & Diseconomies of Scale

content.outcome: Interpret LRAC, Economies & Diseconomies of Scale.
content.core: Long-run average cost shows the lowest attainable cost per unit when every input and plant size can vary. Scale can make specialized tasks and equipment economical, lowering LRAC over a range. Diminishing marginal product is a short-run concept; diseconomies concern scale when all inputs can vary. Falling long-run average cost as output expands is economies of scale.
recognition: Diminishing marginal product is a short-run concept; diseconomies concern scale when all inputs can vary.
A learner reads a downward-sloping LRAC segment as diseconomies of scale.
The concepts apply to different horizons and input changes.
A very large firm becomes harder to coordinate.
content.watch: Do not confuse scale and diminishing returns. Diminishing marginal product is a short-run concept; diseconomies concern scale when all inputs can vary.
content.worked: The LRAC curve falls from about $20 at 30 units to its minimum of about $12 at 60 units, showing economies of scale. It then rises back toward $20 by 90 units, showing diseconomies of scale. The cost-minimizing scale is approximately 60 units.
content.check: The graph gives roughly the same LRAC at Q=30 and Q=90. Which statement distinguishes those two positions?

title: Minimum Efficient Scale & Constant Returns to Scale

content.outcome: Identify Minimum Efficient Scale & Constant Returns to Scale.
content.core: Minimum efficient scale is the smallest output at which long-run average cost reaches its minimum. Before MES, additional scale can still lower long-run average cost; at MES the minimum has been reached. MES summarizes how much output a firm must reach before it captures all available scale economies.
recognition: Find the lowest point of the long-run average-cost curve.
Minimum efficient scale is the smallest output at which that minimum cost is attained.
A flat minimum indicates a range of outputs with constant returns to scale.
Do not confuse a flat average-cost segment with output remaining unchanged.
content.watch: A common mistake is to invent flat lrac region. The graph has a single rounded minimum rather than a visibly flat minimum-cost interval.
content.worked: The LRAC curve reaches its lowest value, about $12 per unit, at an output of 60. Minimum efficient scale is the smallest output that attains minimum long-run average cost, so the graph's MES is 60 units. Outputs below 60 have not exhausted economies of scale.
