title: Market Structure, Price Taking & Firm Revenue

content.outcome: Connect Market Structure, Price Taking & Firm Revenue.
content.core: A perfectly competitive firm takes the market price as given, so price, average revenue, and marginal revenue are equal. Market power changes the firm's revenue conditions; the competitive firm takes price. Price taking makes each sold unit add the same amount to revenue, setting up the later MR-versus-MC output rule.
recognition: Look for many firms, a standardized product, easy entry, and no control over market price.
A price-taking firm can sell another unit without lowering its price.
For the competitive firm, price, average revenue, and marginal revenue are equal.
Treat market price as a horizontal line in the individual firm's graph.
content.watch: A common mistake is to separate price, average revenue, and marginal revenue for a price-taking firm. Under perfect competition, P = AR = MR.
content.worked: The competitive firm takes the market price of $25, so P = MR = AR. The horizontal price line meets marginal cost at 50 units, and total revenue is $25 x 50 = $1,250. Because ATC is also $25 at that output, the firm earns zero economic profit.

title: Profit-Maximizing Output & the MR = MC Rule

content.outcome: Analyze Profit-Maximizing Output & the MR = MC Rule.
content.core: A firm maximizes profit or minimizes loss by producing the quantity where rising marginal cost equals marginal revenue. The local profit maximum occurs where MC rises through MR. Marginal benefit to the firm exceeds marginal cost. Market price becomes the firm’s MR, linking market equilibrium to the firm’s marginal output choice.
recognition: Use the firm's marginal-revenue curve and the rising portion of marginal cost.
Choose the output where marginal cost equals marginal revenue, provided the firm should operate.
If marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost, another unit raises profit; if marginal cost exceeds marginal revenue, it lowers profit.
Do not choose output by minimizing average total cost unless that output also satisfies the marginal rule.
content.watch: A common mistake is to misapply competitive firm rule. Market price becomes the firm’s MR, linking market equilibrium to the firm’s marginal output choice.
content.worked: The firm's market price and marginal revenue are $25. The rising marginal-cost curve reaches $25 at 50 units, so the last unit adds exactly as much revenue as cost. Producing fewer units leaves profitable output unmade; producing more makes MC exceed MR. Profit-maximizing output is 50.

HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT • Use the firm's marginal-revenue curve and the rising portion of marginal cost. • Choose the output where marginal cost equals marginal revenue, provided the firm should operate. • If marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost, another unit raises profit; if marginal cost exceeds marginal revenue, it lowers profit. • Do not choose output by minimizing average total cost unless that output also satisfies the marginal rule. WATCH OUT A common mistake is to misapply competitive firm rule. Market price becomes the firm’s MR, linking market equilibrium to the firm’s marginal output choice. WORKED EXAMPLE: USING THE MR = MC RULE The firm's market price and marginal revenue are $25. The rising marginal-cost curve reaches $25 at 50 units, so the last unit adds exactly as much revenue as cost. Producing fewer units leaves profitable output unmade; producing more makes MC exceed MR. Profit-maximizing output is 50. CHECK YOURSELF MR is $25 and the next unit’s MC is $19. What should the firm do? READY? Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Profit, Loss & Break-Even

content.outcome: Measure Profit, Loss & Break-Even.
content.core: Economic profit or loss equals the gap between price and average total cost multiplied by output. Profit, Loss & Break-Even measures per-unit and total economic profit or loss and interpret break-even and zero economic profit. The firm combines its revenue from price and quantity with all economic costs to measure profit. Profit/loss measurement and the short-run shutdown decision use different comparisons. Separate output, operating status, profit or loss, and long-run entry or exit pressure.
recognition: First find the firm's chosen output using the marginal-revenue and marginal-cost rule.
At that output, compare price with average total cost.
Price above average total cost means profit; equality means break-even; price below average total cost means loss.
Measure profit or loss as the per-unit gap multiplied by output.
content.watch: Do not confuse loss with shutdown. Profit/loss measurement and the short-run shutdown decision use different comparisons. Economic cost includes implicit opportunity costs, including the normal return needed to keep owner resources in the firm.
content.worked: The market sets a price of $15. The representative firm produces 50 units where P = MR = MC, but its ATC is $18. Loss per unit is $18 - $15 = $3, so total loss is $3 x 50 = $150. The firm may still operate because price exceeds AVC.
content.check: How does the price-versus-ATC comparison connect a cost curve to the firm’s profit status?

title: Shutdown & Short-Run Loss Minimization

content.outcome: Apply Shutdown & Short-Run Loss Minimization.
content.core: A firm should operate in the short run when price covers average variable cost, even if price is below average total cost. A lump-sum tax acts like fixed cost. AVC represents avoidable cost in the short run. Short-run loss minimization compares the incremental benefit and avoidable cost of operating.
recognition: Find the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output where marginal revenue equals rising marginal cost.
At that output, compare price with average variable cost.
Operate in the short run when price covers average variable cost; shut down when price falls below it.
A firm may operate at a loss when it covers variable cost and contributes something toward fixed cost.
content.watch: A common mistake is to misapply competitive firm rule. Short-run loss minimization compares the incremental benefit and avoidable cost of operating. A fixed-cost change affects profit and ATC but not MC or AVC, so it does not change the marginal output choice or shutdown threshold.
content.worked: The horizontal price line is $10, below minimum AVC of $20 at point A. At every positive output, revenue per unit would be less than avoidable variable cost. The firm minimizes its short-run loss by shutting down and paying only fixed cost.
content.check: P is below minimum AVC. What should the firm do?

title: Short-Run Supply & Cost Shifts

content.outcome: Analyze Short-Run Supply & Cost Shifts.
content.core: A competitive firm's short-run supply curve is the rising portion of marginal cost at and above minimum average variable cost. The tax is tied to each unit produced. MC gives the additional cost of supply. The short-run supply schedule depends on marginal and variable costs, not fixed cost.
recognition: Use the rising portion of marginal cost at and above minimum average variable cost as firm supply.
A variable-input cost increase shifts marginal cost and short-run supply upward or left.
A fixed-cost change shifts average total cost but leaves marginal cost and short-run supply unchanged.
Distinguish a movement along supply caused by price from a shift caused by production conditions.
content.watch: Do not assume fixed cost shifts supply. The short-run supply schedule depends on marginal and variable costs, not fixed cost. Fixed cost affects profit but not the short-run MC-above-AVC supply schedule.
content.worked: The firm's short-run supply curve is the portion of MC at and above minimum AVC, which begins at point A: 22 units and $20. For example, if market price rises to $30, the firm supplies the quantity at point B, about 33 units. MC below A is not part of supply because the firm shuts down.
content.check: Which MC segment is competitive short-run supply?

title: Entry, Exit & Long-Run Equilibrium

content.outcome: Trace entry, exit, zero economic profit, normal profit, and long-run competitive adjustment.
content.core: Entry and exit move a competitive industry toward long-run equilibrium with zero economic profit. More firms supply more total output at each price. At long-run equilibrium the firm maximizes profit and entry/exit has eliminated economic profit. Entry and exit remove persistent economic profit or loss in the benchmark model.
recognition: At long-run equilibrium the firm maximizes profit and entry/exit has eliminated economic profit.
Entry and exit remove persistent economic profit or loss in the benchmark model.
Long-run industry assessment 10: Demand falls in a constant-cost industry and some firms leave.
Long-run industry assessment 11: Demand rises in a constant-cost industry and entry is unrestricted.
content.watch: Do not miss long run equilibrium conditions. At long-run equilibrium the firm maximizes profit and entry/exit has eliminated economic profit. Entry and exit remove persistent economic profit or loss in the benchmark model.
content.worked: The market equilibrium price is $25. At that price, the representative firm produces 50 units where P = MC, and $25 is also the minimum ATC. Revenue covers all explicit and implicit costs, so economic profit is zero and no entry or exit pressure remains.

title: Long-Run Industry Supply & Cost Conditions

content.outcome: Distinguish Long-Run Industry Supply & Cost Conditions.
content.core: Long-run industry supply depends on how industry expansion changes firms' input costs. The long-run industry response can feed back through shared input markets. The slope depends on how industry expansion affects input costs and firms' cost curves.
recognition: In a constant-cost competitive industry, industry expansion leaves input prices and firms’ cost curves essentially unchanged.
A learner interprets a downward-sloping long-run industry supply curve as a violation of competition.
Short-run market adjustment creates the profit signal; entry and cost conditions determine the long-run destination.
Read only the relationships displayed and apply the competitive-firm sequence in the correct order.
content.watch: Do not confuse industry cost conditions. If expansion does not change input costs, the long-run equilibrium price can return to the original cost level.
content.worked: The long-run industry supply curve slopes upward, rising from roughly $18 at very low output to above $50 near 105 units. Industry expansion therefore raises the long-run equilibrium price. That pattern is consistent with an increasing-cost industry in which entry bids up specialized inputs or other production costs.

title: Competitive Efficiency & Model Limits

content.outcome: Interpret Competitive Efficiency & Model Limits.
content.core: Perfect competition is allocatively efficient when price equals marginal cost and productively efficient when firms produce at minimum average total cost. The benchmark requires private and social marginal costs to align. Apply the exact efficiency conditions and distinguish behavioral assumptions from welfare assumptions. Minimum average total cost represents the least-cost scale for producing that output in the benchmark.
recognition: Apply the exact efficiency conditions and distinguish behavioral assumptions from welfare assumptions.
Minimum average total cost represents the least-cost scale for producing that output in the benchmark.
A representative competitive firm is in long-run equilibrium at the minimum point of ATC.
Price reflects marginal willingness to pay while MC reflects marginal opportunity cost.
content.watch: A common mistake is to equate efficiency with equity. Apply the exact efficiency conditions and distinguish behavioral assumptions from welfare assumptions. Minimum average total cost represents the least-cost scale for producing that output in the benchmark.
content.worked: At the long-run competitive outcome, the firm produces 50 units where price equals marginal cost and price also equals minimum ATC at $25. P = MC gives allocative efficiency, while production at minimum ATC gives productive efficiency. These conclusions depend on the competitive model's assumptions.

title: Monopoly Power, Barriers to Entry & Sources of Monopoly

content.outcome: Identify Monopoly Power, Barriers to Entry & Sources of Monopoly.
content.core: A monopoly has durable market power because barriers prevent close rivals from entering and eroding that power. Barriers can keep profit from triggering the entry response that erodes profit in competitive markets. Natural monopoly can make one-firm production cost-efficient while still creating a market-power problem.
recognition: A city has one coffee shop today, but entry is easy and several rivals are preparing to open.
A software firm is the only seller this year.
The current one-seller market does not by itself establish durable monopoly power.
One seller becomes a durable monopoly only when entry is meaningfully blocked.
content.watch: Do not treat any large firm as monopoly. Durable monopoly power depends on the relevant market and barriers to entry. A monopoly requires meaningful barriers to entry, not merely one seller at a moment in time.
content.worked: Across the relevant output range, the graph's ATC curve declines as output expands, so one large producer can supply the market at lower average cost than several small firms. That cost structure supports natural monopoly. At the efficient point where demand meets MC, price would be below ATC, creating a regulatory funding problem.
content.check: Which fact most strongly supports classifying a firm as a monopoly?

title: Monopoly Demand, Revenue & Marginal Revenue

content.outcome: Interpret Monopoly Demand, Revenue & Marginal Revenue.
content.core: A monopolist faces the market demand curve, so selling another unit requires a lower price and makes marginal revenue less than price. A price taker sells each unit at the same price; a monopolist lowers price to expand output. Price taking removes the price effect that drives monopoly MR below price.
recognition: Start with the monopolist's downward-sloping market demand curve.
Because selling another unit requires a lower price, marginal revenue lies below demand.
For a linear demand curve, marginal revenue shares the vertical intercept and falls twice as quickly.
Marginal revenue is positive where demand is elastic and negative where demand is inelastic.
content.watch: A common mistake is to equate mr and price. Linear MR shares demand’s vertical intercept and is twice as steep. For a downward-sloping demand curve, MR is positive on the elastic portion.
content.worked: At 40 units, the demand curve shows a price of $40, while the marginal-revenue curve shows MR of $20. Total revenue is $40 x 40 = $1,600. The gap between price and marginal revenue illustrates why a monopolist's MR lies below demand when lowering price is necessary to sell another unit.

Difficulty: Intermediate Monopoly Demand, Revenue & Marginal Revenue THE CORE IDEA A monopolist faces the market demand curve, so selling another unit requires a lower price and makes marginal revenue less than price. A price taker sells each unit at the same price; a monopolist lowers price to expand output. Price taking removes the price effect that drives monopoly MR below price. HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT • Start with the monopolist's downward-sloping market demand curve. • Because selling another unit requires a lower price, marginal revenue lies below demand. • For a linear demand curve, marginal revenue shares the vertical intercept and falls twice as quickly. • Marginal revenue is positive where demand is elastic and negative where demand is inelastic. WATCH OUT A common mistake is to equate mr and price. Linear MR shares demand’s vertical intercept and is twice as steep. For a downward-sloping demand curve, MR is positive on the elastic portion. WORKED EXAMPLE: WHY MR FALLS BELOW PRICE At 40 units, the demand curve shows a price of $40, while the marginal-revenue curve shows MR of $20. Total revenue is $40 x 40 = $1,600. The gap between price and marginal revenue illustrates why a monopolist's MR lies below demand when lowering price is necessary to sell another unit. CHECK YOURSELF For a single-price monopolist, which curve gives price at each output? READY? Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Profit-Maximizing Output & Monopoly Price

content.outcome: Apply Profit-Maximizing Output & Monopoly Price.
content.core: A monopolist chooses output where rising marginal cost equals marginal revenue, then uses demand to determine price. Produce units whose marginal revenue covers marginal cost. MR is compared with MC for output choice. Find Q from MR=MC, then read price from demand. Monopoly analysis is a two-step decision: marginal output choice first, demand-based price second.
recognition: Find output where rising marginal cost equals marginal revenue.
Move vertically from that output to the demand curve to find the monopoly price.
Keep the output decision and price decision separate: marginal conditions determine quantity, demand determines price.
Do not set price equal to marginal revenue or marginal cost unless the graph happens to imply it.
content.watch: A common mistake is to read monopoly price from the marginal-revenue curve. Find output where MR = MC, then read the price buyers will pay from demand.
content.worked: The monopolist first finds output where MR = MC, which occurs at 40 units and a marginal value of $20. It then moves up to the demand curve, where buyers will pay $40 for 40 units. The profit-maximizing choice is therefore Q = 40 and P = $40, not the $20 MR value.

title: Monopoly Profit, Loss & Shutdown

content.outcome: Calculate Monopoly Profit, Loss & Shutdown.
content.core: Monopoly profit or loss is measured after the profit-maximizing output and demand-based price have been found. The firm must cover avoidable variable cost. Output optimization and profit measurement are separate steps in monopoly analysis. Profit or loss equals (P−ATC)Q at the chosen output.
recognition: Choose monopoly output where rising marginal cost equals marginal revenue, then read price from demand.
At that output, compare price with average total cost to determine profit or loss.
Compare price with average variable cost to decide whether a loss-making monopolist operates in the short run.
Measure profit or loss as the price-cost gap multiplied by output.
content.watch: A common mistake is to mix output choice with profit measurement. Output optimization and profit measurement are separate steps in monopoly analysis. Profit or loss equals (P−ATC)Q at the chosen output.
content.worked: The firm chooses 36 units where MR equals MC. At that output, demand gives a price of $42 and ATC is $27. Profit per unit is $42 - $27 = $15, so total economic profit is $15 x 36 = $540.
content.check: Why does P>MC not prove positive economic profit?

title: Monopoly Welfare, Efficiency & Competitive Comparison

content.outcome: Compare Monopoly Welfare, Efficiency & Competitive Comparison.
content.core: Compared with competition, monopoly usually restricts output, raises price, transfers surplus, and creates deadweight loss. Transfers remain in total surplus; unrealized trades do not. The omitted units would generate positive gains from trade. Market power generally leads the monopolist to restrict output and charge a higher price than the competitive benchmark.
recognition: Compare monopoly output and price with the competitive benchmark where price equals marginal cost.
Monopoly normally produces less and charges more than a competitive market.
Separate the transfer of surplus to the monopolist from surplus lost through reduced output.
Deadweight loss is the value of trades between monopoly output and the efficient quantity that no longer occur.
content.watch: A common mistake is to reverse monopoly competitive comparison. Market power generally leads the monopolist to restrict output and charge a higher price than the competitive benchmark.
content.worked: The unregulated monopoly chooses about 45 units where MR = MC and charges the demand price of about $47. The efficient outcome occurs where demand meets MC: 90 units at $20. Monopoly therefore restricts output and raises price, leaving mutually beneficial units between 45 and 90 unproduced.
content.check: Which part of lost consumer surplus is deadweight loss?

title: Natural Monopoly & Regulation

content.outcome: Analyze Natural Monopoly & Regulation.
content.core: A natural monopoly has declining average cost across the relevant market range, making one large producer less costly than several small firms. The subsidy addresses the financing gap created by efficient pricing when scale economies keep ATC above MC. Average-cost pricing is a compromise between cost recovery and the P=MC efficiency benchmark. Marginal-cost pricing can require financial support when MC lies below ATC.
recognition: Look for average cost that continues falling across the relevant range of market demand.
Marginal-cost pricing expands output toward efficiency but may leave the firm unable to cover average cost.
Average-cost pricing can preserve financial viability but produces less than the efficient quantity.
Evaluate regulation by comparing price, output, efficiency, and the need for subsidy or allowed profit.
content.watch: Do not confuse allocative efficiency with break even. Marginal-cost pricing can require financial support when MC lies below ATC. Natural monopoly is rooted in cost structure and economies of scale rather than legal exclusion alone.
content.worked: Marginal-cost pricing sets demand equal to MC, which the graph shows at 140 units and $10. ATC there is about $15, so the regulated firm would lose about ($15 - $10) x 140 = $700. Average-cost pricing near 115 units and $16 avoids that loss but leaves price above marginal cost.
content.check: What is the main compromise under average-cost pricing?

title: Price Discrimination

content.outcome: Analyze Price Discrimination.
content.core: Price discrimination charges different buyers different prices for the same product when resale can be prevented. Preventing resale is what allows separated prices to persist. Different demand responsiveness is the economic reason separated groups can receive different optimal prices. Charging each unit up to willingness to pay can make serving all units with value at least MC profitable. Price discrimination requires control over price and a way to distinguish relevant buyers or markets.
recognition: Charging each unit up to willingness to pay can make serving all units with value at least MC profitable.
Price discrimination requires control over price and a way to distinguish relevant buyers or markets.
Perfect discrimination can expand output to the efficient quantity while transferring surplus to the seller.
The firm allocates output across separated markets using marginal revenue relative to marginal cost.
Different demand responsiveness is the economic reason separated groups can receive different optimal prices.
content.watch: A common mistake is to disconnect wtp from first degree efficiency. Charging each unit up to willingness to pay can make serving all units with value at least MC profitable.
content.worked: A theater charges students $8 and other adults $14 for the same seat. The policy can persist only if students cannot resell discounted tickets to adults; otherwise arbitrage would erase the price difference. Verification separates the groups, and the different prices reflect different demand elasticities.
content.check: Can ordinary group price discrimination increase total welfare?

title: Market Structure & Product Differentiation

content.outcome: Identify Market Structure & Product Differentiation.
content.core: Monopolistic competition combines many firms and relatively easy entry with differentiated products and limited price-setting power. Entry and exit operate in both models. Differentiation explains why an individual firm faces downward-sloping demand despite many sellers and easy entry. The practice is differentiating the service experience rather than relying on a legal barrier or identical product. Differentiation makes the firm’s product an imperfect substitute, so its individual demand curve slopes downward.
recognition: A market has many sellers and easy entry.
A dental practice competes mainly through evening hours, online scheduling, and unusually fast appointments.
A restaurant has many nearby rivals, but customers value its menu and atmosphere enough that a small price increase does not drive everyone away.
A market has many small sellers and easy entry, but every seller offers exactly the same product.
A neighborhood café competes through atmosphere, menu, and location.
content.watch: A common mistake is to misapply monopolistic competition rule. Differentiation explains why an individual firm faces downward-sloping demand despite many sellers and easy entry.
content.worked: A city has many coffee shops, entry is relatively easy, and each shop offers a distinct menu and atmosphere. Because customers view the shops as close but imperfect substitutes, each shop faces downward-sloping demand and has limited price-setting power. Those facts identify monopolistic competition.
content.check: Why is a differentiated firm’s demand downward sloping?

title: Short-Run Firm Choice, Profit/Loss & Shutdown

content.outcome: Use Short-Run Firm Choice, Profit/Loss & Shutdown.
content.core: Short-Run Firm Choice, Profit/Loss & Shutdown uses MR = MC, firm demand, ATC, and AVC to determine output, price, profit or loss, and short-run shutdown. The firm shuts down when price cannot cover variable cost. At the chosen output, price above ATC means profit, price below ATC means loss, and equality means zero economic profit.
recognition: Use marginal revenue and rising marginal cost to choose the firm's output.
Read price and average total cost at that output to determine profit or loss.
Use average variable cost to determine whether the firm operates or shuts down in the short run.
Keep output choice, profit measurement, and shutdown analysis as three distinct steps.

content.worked: The firm chooses 36 units where MR = MC at $15, then charges $27 on its demand curve. ATC is also $27, so total revenue and total cost are both $27 x 36 = $972. Economic profit is zero, but P > MC shows the outcome is not allocatively efficient.

title: Entry, Exit & Long-Run Equilibrium

content.outcome: Trace Entry, Exit & Long-Run Equilibrium.
content.core: In monopolistic competition, short-run profit attracts entry and short-run loss causes exit until economic profit is zero. Entry and exit remove economic profit in both models. Excess capacity compares equilibrium Q with minimum-ATC Q.
recognition: Short-run economic profit attracts entry, which reduces each incumbent firm's demand.
Short-run losses cause exit, which raises the demand facing surviving firms.
Long-run equilibrium occurs when the firm's demand is tangent to average total cost and economic profit is zero.
Distinguish zero economic profit from zero accounting profit.
content.watch: A common mistake is to equate zero economic and accounting profit. Entry and exit remove economic profit in both models. Zero economic profit is an entry condition, not proof of allocative or productive efficiency.
content.worked: At 36 units, the firm charges $27 and has ATC of $27. Total revenue is $27 x 36 = $972, and total cost is also $972, so economic profit is zero. With no profit attracting entry and no loss causing exit, the industry is in long-run equilibrium.

title: Advertising, Branding & Nonprice Competition

content.outcome: Analyze Advertising, Branding & Nonprice Competition.
content.core: Advertising can provide information, persuade buyers, build a brand, and change the elasticity or position of a firm's demand curve. The firm is competing through product features and service rather than changing price. In signaling models, willingness to incur a visible selling cost can sometimes convey information when higher quality supports repeat sales. A fixed selling cost raises fixed and average total cost but does not directly raise MC or AVC. The ad is trying to shape preferences and brand perception rather than mainly transmit facts.
recognition: A shoe company introduces custom colors and faster delivery while leaving its posted price unchanged.
Consumers cannot directly observe product durability before purchase.
A firm buys a one-time advertising campaign that does not change demand.
A perfume ad links the brand with status and excitement but provides almost no factual product information.
A branding campaign leaves the number of buyers unchanged but makes them less price sensitive.

title: Oligopoly Structure, Strategic Interdependence & Concentration

content.outcome: Identify Oligopoly Structure, Strategic Interdependence & Concentration.
content.core: An oligopoly contains only a few important firms, so each firm's decisions depend on expected rival responses. With only a few important firms, one firm’s action can provoke responses that change its own payoff.
recognition: Look for a market dominated by a few firms with meaningful barriers to entry.
Each firm's price, output, or advertising decision depends on how rivals are expected to respond.
Use concentration measures as evidence about structure, not as a complete verdict about competition.
The defining clue is strategic interdependence among the important firms.
content.watch: Do not use firm count alone. Dominant shares and strategic interdependence point to oligopoly. Concentration depends on the boundaries of the relevant market.

title: Game Theory Foundations: Payoff Matrices, Best Responses & Nash Equilibrium

content.outcome: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibrium.
content.core: Game theory represents strategic choices with players, actions, and payoffs that depend on what others do. Correctly reading the matrix is the prerequisite for identifying best responses and equilibrium. Compare mutual best responses with the combined-payoff maximum. A Nash equilibrium is a cell containing mutual best responses.
recognition: Identify the players, each player's available actions, and the payoff associated with every action combination.
For each possible rival action, mark the action that gives a player the highest payoff.
A dominant strategy is best regardless of the rival's action.
A Nash equilibrium is a cell where every player's action is a best response to the others.
content.watch: Do not assume equilibrium is efficient. Compare mutual best responses with the combined-payoff maximum. A Nash equilibrium is a cell containing mutual best responses.
content.worked: For each rival strategy, identify the action with the larger payoff. If column X is chosen, row A gives 9 rather than 3 from row B. If column Y is chosen, row A gives 2 rather than 1 from row B. Thus, A is the row player's strictly dominant strategy. For the column player, X gives 9 rather than 3 when row A is chosen, and 2 rather than 1 when row B is chosen. Thus, X is the column player's strictly dominant strategy. Because A and X are mutual best responses, (A, X) is the unique Nash equilibrium.

title: Collusion, Cartels & Prisoner's-Dilemma Incentives

content.outcome: Analyze Collusion, Cartels & Prisoner's-Dilemma Incentives.
content.core: A cartel coordinates firms to restrict industry output and raise price as a monopolist would. Individual incentives can push both firms toward a lower-payoff noncooperative outcome. The conflict is between individual and collective incentives. A prisoner’s dilemma exists precisely because individual incentives can undermine a jointly better outcome.
recognition: Individual incentives can push both firms toward a lower-payoff noncooperative outcome.
The conflict is between individual and collective incentives.
A prisoner’s dilemma exists precisely because individual incentives can undermine a jointly better outcome.
Three firms agree to keep prices high.
content.watch: Do not miss individual incentive to defect. The conflict is between individual and collective incentives. Private incentives can conflict with the cartel’s collective restriction.
content.worked: A cartel acts like one monopolist and selects industry output where industry MR equals MC. On the graph, the downward-sloping MR curve meets the $20 MC line at 20 units. The cartel then uses demand to set price. Each member has an incentive to sell extra units, which makes the agreement unstable.

title: Dynamic Strategy: Repeated Games, Credibility & Entry Deterrence

content.outcome: Analyze repeated games, credible commitments, entry deterrence, and sequential strategic choices.
content.core: Dynamic Strategy: Repeated Games, Credibility & Entry Deterrence examines repeated interaction, credibility, commitments, limit pricing, entry deterrence, continuation incentives, and sequential strategic reasoning. Aggressive competition and predation must be distinguished with evidence.

title: Tacit Coordination, Price Leadership & Nonprice Competition

content.outcome: Analyze Tacit Coordination, Price Leadership & Nonprice Competition.
content.core: Tacit coordination occurs when firms align behavior without an explicit agreement, while nonprice competition uses quality, service, or advertising rather than price cuts. Advertising can shape demand in both markets. Strategic interdependence applies to quality, advertising, service, and other competitive dimensions as well as price. Tacit coordination refers to aligned behavior without the explicit agreement that defines collusion.
recognition: A student has learned that oligopoly firms react strategically to price changes.
A student says tacit coordination and explicit collusion are identical.
Tacit coordination can arise through expectations and repeated conduct.
A firm increases product quality rather than cutting price.
content.watch: Do not assume price is irrelevant. Oligopolists can compete on quality and other dimensions. A leader’s announced price can become a focal point.
content.worked: The kink in demand occurs near 20 units and a price of $50. Because the marginal-revenue curve has a gap at that output, modest changes in MC around $36 need not change the chosen price or quantity. The model explains price rigidity while reminding us that oligopolists can still compete through quality, service, and advertising.

title: Oligopoly Welfare, Mergers & Antitrust Tradeoffs

content.outcome: Evaluate Oligopoly Welfare, Mergers & Antitrust Tradeoffs.
content.core: Oligopoly and merger policy weighs the risk of reduced rivalry against verifiable efficiencies, innovation, entry, and consumer effects. Policy weighs market-power risk against verifiable benefits. A sound evaluation combines structure, strategic conduct, efficiency claims, and market responses. The core welfare concern is reduced rivalry that raises prices, restricts output, and can create deadweight loss. Oligopoly welfare requires integrating several margins rather than treating one statistic as decisive.
recognition: A sound evaluation combines structure, strategic conduct, efficiency claims, and market responses.
The core welfare concern is reduced rivalry that raises prices, restricts output, and can create deadweight loss.
A concentrated industry has high prices, strong product innovation, and frequent entry by niche rivals.
A student sees several firms charge the same price and immediately labels the behavior collusion.
A merger creates a larger research budget but also reduces head-to-head price competition.
content.watch: A common mistake is to equate cartel profit with dwl. DWL is the triangle between demand and MC over the lost output. Oligopoly policy requires evidence about conduct, entry, efficiencies, and consumer effects.
content.worked: A merger raises the HHI and may increase market power, but the statistic alone is not the verdict. Suppose the merged firm can cut marginal cost by $4 per unit and entry remains easy. An antitrust evaluation compares the likely price and output effects of reduced rivalry with the verifiable efficiency and entry evidence before reaching a conclusion.

title: Externalities

content.outcome: Compare private and social incentives and identify the efficient quantity.
content.core: An externality is a cost or benefit imposed on someone outside a transaction. Negative externalities make private decision makers ignore part of social cost; positive externalities make them ignore part of social benefit. Efficiency uses all marginal social costs and benefits.
recognition: Ask whether the spillover is a cost or benefit and whether it comes from production or consumption.
Negative: MSC > MPC or MPB > MSB, so the market quantity is too high.
Positive: MSB > MPB or MPC > MSC, so the market quantity is too low.
Corrective taxes, subsidies, permits, regulation, or bargaining can internalize the spillover.
content.watch: Do not label every harmful outcome an externality. A spillover must affect a third party and be missing from the market price.
content.worked: Fast-fashion production creates a $6 external cost per garment, so MSC lies $6 above MPC. The market produces 240 million garments where MPB = MPC at $12. Efficiency occurs at 160 million garments where MPB = MSC at $15, eliminating 80 million units of overproduction. A $6 corrective tax aligns private and social marginal cost.

title: Public Goods & Common Resources

content.outcome: Classify goods and apply efficient provision and resource-use rules.
content.core: Excludability asks whether nonpayers can be kept out; rivalry asks whether one person's use reduces another's. Public goods are nonexcludable and nonrival, common resources are nonexcludable and rival, club goods are excludable and nonrival, and private goods are excludable and rival.
recognition: Free riding can make private payments understate total social willingness to pay for a public good.
Vertically sum individual marginal benefits to obtain MSB for a shared quantity.
Provide the efficient public-good quantity where MSB = MC.
Common resources tend toward overuse; property rights, access rules, or practical exclusion can change incentives.
content.watch: Do not classify a good by who supplies it. Government provision does not automatically make a good nonexcludable or nonrival.
content.worked: At four community fireworks displays, North's marginal benefit is $30,000 and South's is $20,000. Because both communities consume the same shared quantity, MSB is the vertical sum: $50,000. MC is also $50,000, so four displays are efficient. Summing quantities horizontally would be incorrect.

HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT - Free riding can make private payments understate total social willingness to pay for a public good. - Vertically sum individual marginal benefits to obtain MSB for a shared quantity. - Provide the efficient public-good quantity where MSB = MC. - Common resources tend toward overuse; property rights, access rules, or practical exclusion can change incentives. ! WATCH OUT Do not classify a good by who supplies it. Government provision does not automatically make a good nonexcludable or nonrival. # WORKED EXAMPLE: VERTICAL SUMMATION At four community fireworks displays, North's marginal benefit is $30,000 and South's is $20,000. Because both communities consume the same shared quantity, MSB is the vertical sum: $50,000. MC is also $50,000, so four displays are efficient. Summing quantities horizontally would be incorrect. ? CHECK YOURSELF Which combination describes a common resource: excludable/nonrival or nonexcludable/rival? READY? Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Market Power

content.outcome: Explain how limited competition lets a firm influence price and efficiency.
content.core: Market power is the ability to influence price rather than take the market price as given. It can arise from barriers to entry, product differentiation, control of a key input, network effects, or a small number of rivals. Monopoly is one strong case, but market power is broader than monopoly.
recognition: A price-setting firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve for its product.
Barriers or limited substitutes reduce competitive pressure and protect markups.
Compared with a competitive benchmark, market power commonly raises price and reduces output.
The output restriction can create deadweight loss because mutually beneficial trades do not occur.
content.watch: Do not infer market power from a high price alone. Look for limited substitution, entry barriers, concentration, or evidence that the firm can profitably influence price.
content.worked: A local utility is protected by very high fixed network costs, so duplicating the network is inefficient. The firm can influence price because entry is difficult. Regulation may limit the price, but a price set too low can also prevent cost recovery. The central issue is the tradeoff between market power and feasible service provision.
content.check: Why can a firm with close substitutes usually exercise less market power?

title: Factor Markets & Labor Demand

content.outcome: Use marginal productivity to analyze labor demand, wages, and employment.
content.core: Labor demand is derived from the value workers add to output. Marginal product of labor is the extra output from one more worker. For a price-taking seller, VMP = output price x MPL. A profit-maximizing firm hires labor up to the point where VMP equals the wage.
recognition: A wage change causes movement along labor demand; productivity or output-price changes shift labor demand.
Higher product demand, output price, or worker productivity shifts labor demand right.
Worker preferences, population, migration, training, and alternative jobs can shift labor supply.
Competitive wage and employment occur where market labor demand intersects market labor supply.
content.watch: Do not confuse MPL with VMP. MPL is extra physical output; VMP converts that output into dollars by multiplying by the output price.
content.worked: Warehouse labor demand and labor supply intersect at an hourly wage of $20 and 40 hundreds of workers. Because the horizontal axis is measured in hundreds, equilibrium employment is 4,000 workers. Below $20, firms demand more labor than workers supply; above $20, labor supplied exceeds labor demanded.
content.check: If the output price rises while worker productivity is unchanged, what happens to labor demand?

title: Consumer Choice

content.outcome: Use a budget constraint and preferences to identify the best affordable bundle.
content.core: A budget constraint shows every bundle a consumer can afford at given income and prices. Its intercepts are income divided by each good's price, and its slope is the negative relative price. Preferences rank feasible bundles; the optimum is the highest attainable indifference curve, usually where MRS equals the price ratio.
recognition: Bundles inside or on the budget line are feasible; bundles outside it are infeasible.
An income change shifts the line in parallel when prices are fixed.
A change in one price pivots the line around the unchanged intercept.
At an interior optimum, marginal utility per dollar is equal across goods.
content.watch: Spending the whole budget is not enough to prove optimality. The chosen bundle must also provide the highest attainable preference ranking.
content.worked: The budget line reaches 20 units of X or 40 units of Y, so its slope is -2. Bundle A contains 10 units of X and 20 of Y. At A, the budget line is tangent to IC2, the highest attainable indifference curve. IC3 is preferred but lies outside the feasible set, while IC1 is attainable but provides a lower ranking.
content.check: If only the price of Y falls, does the budget line shift in parallel or pivot?

title: Income Inequality & the Lorenz Curve

content.outcome: Interpret Lorenz curves, Gini coefficients, and redistribution tradeoffs.
content.core: A Lorenz curve plots the cumulative share of income received by cumulative shares of the population, ordered from lowest to highest income. The 45-degree line represents complete equality. A curve farther below that line indicates greater inequality, not necessarily lower average income.
recognition: Read a point as a cumulative population share paired with a cumulative income share.
A Lorenz curve moving toward the equality line indicates less inequality.
The Gini coefficient summarizes the gap from equality: 0 is equality; values nearer 1 indicate more inequality.
Poverty thresholds and redistribution policies address related but distinct questions from inequality measurement.
content.watch: Do not use a Lorenz curve to infer a country's income level. Two countries can have the same distribution shape and very different average incomes.
content.worked: Before transfers, the bottom 40 percent receives 15 percent of income. After transfers, its share rises to 22 percent and the Lorenz curve moves closer to equality. The displayed Gini falls from 0.380 to 0.252. These changes indicate less relative inequality, but do not show whether total or average income rose.
content.check: Which society is more unequal: the one with Gini 0.28 or Gini 0.46?

title: Adverse Selection

content.outcome: Identify hidden-information problems that arise before an agreement or transaction.
content.core: Adverse selection arises when one side has private information about characteristics or risk before an agreement. Because prices or terms cannot fully reflect each type, higher-risk or higher-cost participants may be more likely to enter, changing the market pool.
recognition: Look for hidden characteristics or risk known by one party before agreement.
The informed and uninformed sides value the transaction differently because information is unequal.
When one price covers many types, high-risk or high-cost types may participate disproportionately.
The pool can worsen, raising prices, reducing coverage, or eliminating beneficial trade.
content.watch: Do not confuse adverse selection with moral hazard. Adverse selection is hidden information before agreement; moral hazard is hidden action or changed behavior after protection.
content.worked: An insurer cannot perfectly observe applicants' health risk before enrollment, so it charges one premium based on average expected cost. Risk type already exists before coverage. Higher-risk applicants find the policy more attractive and enroll at a higher rate. The insured pool's expected cost rises, so the insurer may raise premiums or reduce coverage. Those responses can drive more low-risk buyers away, worsening selection.
content.check: An applicant conceals a chronic condition before enrolling. Does the information problem occur before or after agreement?

title: Moral Hazard

content.outcome: Identify how protection or a contract can change behavior after an agreement.
content.core: Moral hazard occurs when protection from some consequences changes a person's actions after an agreement, while those actions are difficult for the other party to observe or control. The protection changes incentives rather than merely revealing a preexisting type.
recognition: Coverage, a guarantee, or another agreement is already in place.
Behavior changes afterward because the person bears less of the consequence.
The relevant action or precaution is imperfectly observed or controlled.
Insurance, lending, employment, and guarantees can create this incentive.
content.watch: Moral hazard is not simply bad behavior. Protection must change incentives after agreement. Hidden characteristics that exist before agreement instead point to adverse selection.
content.worked: A driver obtains collision insurance with a very low deductible. Coverage comes first. Because the insurer now pays most damage costs, the driver bears less of the financial consequence and becomes less careful about where the car is parked. That reduced incentive for precaution can raise expected losses. The mechanism is moral hazard because behavior changes after protection, not because the driver's type was hidden beforehand.
content.check: After receiving a loan guarantee, a borrower chooses a riskier project. Does that change illustrate moral hazard?

title: Signaling & Screening

content.outcome: Distinguish who initiates an information-revealing action in an asymmetric-information market.
content.core: Markets use actions and information-gathering mechanisms to reduce asymmetric information. Signaling begins with the informed party, who sends credible information. Screening begins with the uninformed party, who requests evidence or designs choices that help reveal type.
recognition: Signals come from the informed side: credentials, warranties, certifications, or reputation investment.
Screens come from the uninformed side: tests, interviews, credit checks, or medical exams.
A menu of contracts can screen when choices reveal otherwise hidden information.
Ask who initiated the information-revealing action, not merely what information appeared.
content.watch: Do not classify the mechanism from the evidence alone. The same fact can be disclosed voluntarily as a signal or requested by the uninformed side as a screen.
content.worked: A job applicant knows more about personal skill than an employer. The applicant earns a certification to demonstrate ability: the informed applicant initiates the action, so it is signaling. The employer then requires every applicant to complete a skills test: the uninformed employer initiates the information request, so it is screening. Direction of action, not the labor-market setting, distinguishes the mechanisms.
content.check: A lender requires borrowers to provide income documentation. Is the lender signaling or screening?

title: Present Bias

content.outcome: Recognize choices that place disproportionate weight on immediate costs or benefits.
content.core: Present bias occurs when people give unusually strong weight to rewards or costs in the immediate present relative to future consequences. It can produce procrastination, undersaving, and repeated plans to act later that are abandoned when later becomes now.
recognition: Look for a conflict between what a person plans for later and chooses now.
Immediate gratification or an immediate cost receives disproportionate weight.
Beneficial actions such as saving, studying, or preventive care are repeatedly postponed.
Commitment devices and well-designed defaults can help counter the bias.
content.watch: Preferring an earlier reward is not automatically present bias. The defining clue is an extra, disproportionate weight on the immediate present, often visible in preference reversals.
content.worked: A worker values retirement saving and repeatedly plans to increase contributions next month. Yet each payday, immediate consumption receives extra weight, so the worker spends the money and postpones saving again. The future goal is valued, but behavior reverses when the choice becomes immediate. Automatic enrollment or a binding contribution commitment can prevent the repeated delay.
content.check: A student plans to begin studying tomorrow but makes the same choice to delay each evening. What clue indicates present bias?

title: Loss Aversion

content.outcome: Recognize when an equal-sized loss affects choice more strongly than a gain.
content.core: Loss aversion means that people often experience a loss as more consequential than an equal-sized gain, measured relative to a reference point. This asymmetry can make giving something up feel more important than acquiring the same amount.
recognition: Identify the reference point that separates a perceived gain from a perceived loss.
Compare reactions to changes of equal magnitude in opposite directions.
Reluctance to give up something already owned can reflect the same asymmetry.
The key evidence is stronger weight on the loss, not simply dislike of uncertainty.
content.watch: Loss aversion is not identical to risk aversion. Risk aversion concerns uncertainty; loss aversion concerns asymmetric reactions to losses and equivalent gains around a reference point.
content.worked: A student uses the expected account balance as a reference point. An unexpected $50 refund produces mild pleasure, while an unexpected $50 fee produces much greater distress. The dollar changes are equal in magnitude, but the $50 loss receives greater psychological weight than the $50 gain. That asymmetry around the reference point is evidence of loss aversion.
content.check: Someone is much more upset by losing $20 than pleased by gaining $20. Which comparison supports loss aversion?

title: Framing Effects

content.outcome: Recognize when equivalent choices produce different decisions because of their description.
content.core: A framing effect occurs when presenting economically equivalent information in different ways changes choice. A gain frame and a loss frame can draw attention to different features even though the underlying outcomes are the same or nearly the same.
recognition: First verify that the underlying outcomes are economically equivalent or nearly equivalent.
Compare gain wording with loss wording, such as survival versus mortality.
Equivalent discounts and surcharges can also create different reactions through framing.
A changed choice caused by presentation, rather than outcomes, is the diagnostic clue.
content.watch: Framing requires equivalent underlying alternatives. If costs, probabilities, or consequences actually differ, a different choice may be rational rather than a framing effect.
content.worked: A treatment is described to one group as having a 90% survival rate and to another as having a 10% mortality rate. The probabilities describe the same outcome. If acceptance changes merely because one statement emphasizes survival and the other emphasizes death, the wording—not an economic difference—changed choice. That response is a framing effect.
content.check: A fee is described either as a $5 surcharge or as losing a $5 discount. If the net price is identical, what mechanism may change choice?

title: Condorcet Paradox & Voting Cycles

content.outcome: Explain how pairwise majority rule can generate cyclic collective preferences.
content.core: Even when every voter has a consistent ranking, pairwise majority voting can produce a cycle: A defeats B, B defeats C, and C defeats A. The group then has no option that defeats every alternative, and agenda order can affect the final outcome.
recognition: There are at least three alternatives and voters rank them differently.
Compare alternatives two at a time using majority rule.
The collective relation cycles even though each individual's ranking is consistent.
Because no option is a universal majority winner, agenda order may matter.
content.watch: A voting cycle does not require irrational voters. Individually transitive rankings can aggregate into an intransitive majority relation.
content.worked: Voter 1 ranks A > B > C; Voter 2 ranks B > C > A; Voter 3 ranks C > A > B. Against B, A wins with Voters 1 and 3. Against C, B wins with Voters 1 and 2. Against A, C wins with Voters 2 and 3. Thus the majority relation is A > B > C > A, so the agenda can determine which comparison occurs last and which option survives.
content.check: Why can changing the order of pairwise votes change the winner when majority preferences form a cycle?

title: Arrow's Impossibility Theorem

content.outcome: Explain the basic limitation on combining individual rankings into a social ranking.
content.core: With at least three alternatives, Arrow's theorem shows that no ranked-choice social decision rule can guarantee all of a specified set of desirable conditions at once. The result identifies a tradeoff among aggregation properties; it does not prove that democracy or every voting system is impossible.
recognition: The problem combines individual rankings into a complete and consistent social ranking.
Desirable conditions include respecting unanimity and avoiding control by one dictator.
Independence of irrelevant alternatives limits how an outside option may change a pairwise ranking.
The theorem concerns simultaneous guarantees under its conditions, not whether voting can occur.
content.watch: Do not conclude that no voting system works or that democracy is impossible. The theorem applies to ranked aggregation and the simultaneous satisfaction of specified conditions.
content.worked: A community wants a ranked-choice rule that respects unanimous rankings, is not controlled by one voter, produces a consistent social ranking, and treats irrelevant alternatives appropriately. Each property seems reasonable. Arrow's theorem says that, with at least three alternatives and unrestricted individual rankings, no aggregation rule can guarantee all of them simultaneously. The lesson is an unavoidable design tradeoff, not a claim that collective choice is meaningless.
content.check: Which is accurate: Arrow identifies incompatible guarantees under stated conditions, or proves that no election can produce a winner?

title: Median Voter Theorem

content.outcome: Explain why majority-rule competition can favor the median voter's position under specific assumptions.
content.core: When policy lies on one dimension, preferences are single-peaked, and decisions use majority rule, the median voter's preferred position has a special advantage. Policies or candidates may move toward it because alternatives on either side can be defeated by a majority.
recognition: Place voters along one policy dimension and identify the middle preferred position.
Each voter has a single peak and prefers positions less as they move away from it.
Pairwise decisions use majority rule.
Competition can favor the median, but the conclusion depends on these assumptions.
content.watch: The median voter does not always decide elections. Multidimensional policy, non-single-peaked preferences, turnout, institutions, or other departures can break the result.
content.worked: Five voters prefer policy levels 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50. The ordered middle preference is 30. Against a proposal below 30, the voters at 30, 40, and 50 form a majority for 30; against one above 30, the voters at 10, 20, and 30 form a majority for 30. Under one-dimensional, single-peaked preferences and majority rule, the median position can defeat alternatives on either side.
content.check: For preferred policies 5, 15, 25, 35, and 45, which position is median, and what preference assumption is required?

title: GDP Measurement

content.outcome: Apply GDP inclusion rules and explain why measured expenditure equals measured income
content.core: Gross domestic product is the market value of final goods and services produced within a country's borders during a specific period. Current production matters: used goods, stocks, bonds, and transfer payments do not represent newly produced output. Final goods are counted instead of adding intermediate goods separately, because the intermediate value is already included in the final product. The location of production, not the owner's nationality, determines whether output is domestic. Measured expenditure equals measured income because a buyer's spending becomes income to the sellers and workers who produced the output.
recognition: The good or service was produced during the period being measured.
Production occurred inside the country's borders, regardless of ownership.
A final product is distinguished from an input used to make another product.
A resale, financial trade, or transfer changes ownership but adds no current output.
One transaction is viewed as both buyer expenditure and seller income.
content.watch: Spending money does not automatically create GDP. A used-car sale, stock purchase, or cash transfer may be a transaction without current production. Also, adding the value of an intermediate input and the final good double counts the input. Imports are excluded because they were produced abroad, even when domestic residents buy them.
content.worked: A mill sells flour to a bakery for $50, and the bakery sells the finished bread to households for $120. Final-goods accounting counts $120, not $170, because the flour's value is already embodied in the bread. The households' $120 of expenditure becomes revenue and income for the producers involved. Counting the same production from the expenditure side or the income side therefore gives the same GDP amount.
content.check: A U.S.-owned factory makes a car in Mexico, while a Japanese-owned factory makes a car in Ohio. Which car belongs in U.S. GDP, and what rule determines the answer?

title: GDP Components

content.outcome: Calculate consumption, investment, government purchases, and net exports.
content.core: The expenditure approach divides GDP into consumption, investment, government purchases, and net exports. Consumption covers household purchases of final goods and services; investment includes business capital, residential construction, and inventory changes; government purchases pay for current goods and services. Net exports add exports and subtract imports so GDP counts only domestic production, while transfer payments themselves are excluded. A recipient's later purchase is counted separately if it pays for current domestic output.
recognition: Classify final spending as consumption, investment, government purchases, or net exports.
Count newly produced capital goods and inventory changes as investment.
Exclude transfer payments because they are not payments for current production.
Subtract imports within net exports so foreign production is not counted in domestic GDP.
content.watch: A common mistake is to count transfer payments as government purchases. Transfers redistribute income and are never themselves part of GDP. A later purchase is classified by what is bought; imports are subtracted in NX.
content.worked: A business buys a newly produced domestic machine for $2 million; this is investment. Government pays contractors $80 million to repair roads; this is government purchases. An $80 million benefit payment is a transfer and is not counted when sent, though any later household purchase of final goods enters consumption. The expenditure identity classifies the counted spending as C + I + G + NX.
content.check: Does a government benefit payment enter G when it is sent?

title: Real versus Nominal GDP

content.outcome: Distinguish nominal and real GDP and calculate the GDP deflator.
content.core: Nominal GDP values current production at current prices, while real GDP values it at base-year prices. Multiply current quantities by the designated base-year prices and add across final goods. GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare. Compare nominal and real GDP to separate price changes from changes in production. Real-GDP growth equals the change in real GDP divided by the initial real GDP.
recognition: Nominal GDP uses current-year prices and current-year quantities.
Real GDP uses base-year prices with current-year quantities.
A change in nominal GDP can reflect prices, quantities, or both; a change in real GDP reflects quantities.
Use the GDP deflator to compare nominal GDP with real GDP for the same year.
content.watch: Do not use the new level rather than the initial real-GDP level as the percentage-growth denominator. Real-GDP growth equals the change in real GDP divided by the initial real GDP.
content.worked: An economy produces 100 units in the base year at $5 each and 110 units this year at $6 each. Nominal GDP this year is 110 x $6 = $660. Real GDP at base-year prices is 110 x $5 = $550. The GDP deflator is ($660 / $550) x 100 = 120, separating the price increase from the output increase.
content.check: Is real GDP calculated by simply subtracting the inflation rate from nominal GDP?

title: Limits of GDP

content.outcome: Evaluate GDP as a measure of well-being.
content.core: GDP measures market production, not every dimension of well-being. GDP can rise from replacement activity even if people are worse off. GDP is useful, but it is not a complete measure of well-being. Moving activity into or out of markets can change GDP even when useful services or consumer benefit move differently. GDP is useful because income matters, but it leaves out things like leisure, environmental quality, and some nonmarket activity.
recognition: A family replaces unpaid home cooking with otherwise similar restaurant meals.
Unpaid elder care becomes an otherwise similar paid service.
A country has higher GDP, but also more pollution and longer work hours.
A free digital service replaces a paid service while users receive greater benefit.
A free technology replaces paid translation services, measured GDP falls, and users translate more text with less effort.
content.watch: A common mistake is to equate a change in market spending with the same change in total useful services. Moving activity into or out of markets can change GDP even when useful services or consumer benefit move differently.
content.worked: A hurricane destroys homes, and rebuilding adds $2 billion to measured construction. Holding other domestic production constant, rebuilding adds $2 billion to GDP. It does not subtract the homes that were destroyed or the loss of security and leisure, so the GDP increase does not prove that well-being improved.

title: CPI and Inflation Measurement

content.outcome: Calculate CPI and inflation using a market basket.
content.core: The consumer price index compares the current cost of a fixed consumer basket with its base-year cost. The index equals the current basket cost divided by the base-year basket cost, multiplied by one hundred. Inflation is the percentage change in the index between periods. Holding basket quantities fixed isolates price change from changes in what consumers buy.
recognition: Identify the fixed basket, its base-year cost, and its current-year cost.
Compute the price index by comparing the current basket cost with the base-year basket cost.
Measure inflation as the percentage change in the index from one period to the next.
Keep basket quantities fixed when calculating the CPI for different years.
content.watch: Do not use the wrong basket cost or forget to multiply by 100. Divide the current cost of the fixed basket by its base-year cost; the index can rise or fall as prices change.
content.worked: The CPI rises from 125 to 150. The inflation rate is (150 - 125)/125 x 100 = 20%. In a separate basket, base-year cost is 4($10) + 2($20) = $80 and current cost is 4($12) + 2($25) = $98, so CPI is ($98/$80) x 100 = 122.5.
content.check: A basket costs $400 in the base year and $500 today. What is today's CPI?

title: CPI Bias

content.outcome: Analyze substitution, quality, and new-goods bias.
content.core: The CPI can overstate changes in the cost of living when a fixed basket misses substitution, quality improvements, or new goods. Substitution bias arises when consumers shift toward relatively cheaper alternatives but the fixed basket does not fully reflect that response. CPI remains useful, while substitution, new-good, and quality challenges can make measured inflation differ from true cost-of-living growth. If goods improve in quality, price increases may overstate the rise in the cost of living. If consumers substitute, their actual cost of living may rise less than the fixed basket suggests.
recognition: If goods improve in quality, price increases may overstate the rise in the cost of living.
If consumers substitute, their actual cost of living may rise less than the fixed basket suggests.
A new product gives consumers a useful option that did not previously exist.
A product becomes more expensive but also much higher quality.
A laptop price rises while speed and battery life improve.
content.watch: Do not treat all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves. If goods improve in quality, price increases may overstate the rise in the cost of living.
content.worked: A fixed basket contains beef even after beef prices rise sharply. Consumers substitute toward chicken, but the CPI continues pricing the original beef quantity. Because the fixed basket misses that cost-saving response, measured inflation can exceed the increase in the cost of maintaining consumers' actual purchasing pattern.
content.check: A refrigerator sells for the same price but uses much less electricity and lasts longer. Which CPI issue matters?

title: CPI versus GDP Deflator

content.outcome: Compare the construction and uses of CPI and the GDP deflator.
content.core: The CPI tracks prices paid for a consumer basket, while the GDP deflator tracks prices of currently produced domestic final output. Imported consumer goods affect CPI but not the GDP deflator directly. Use CPI for consumer purchasing-power questions and the GDP deflator for the price level of current domestic GDP. Identify the buyer and production location, then match the price change to the index whose scope includes it. CPI follows a consumer-basket framework; the GDP deflator follows prices of current domestically produced final output.
recognition: Use CPI for consumer purchasing-power questions and the GDP deflator for the price level of current domestic GDP.
A domestic firm buys newly produced business software whose price rises.
Imported prescription-drug prices rise while prices of domestic hospital services are unchanged.
A city buys domestic transit vehicles while households buy imported fuel.
Domestic food-export prices rise and imported-clothing prices fall.
content.watch: Do not treat CPI and the GDP deflator as interchangeable measures of the same set of prices. CPI follows a consumer-basket framework; the GDP deflator follows prices of current domestically produced final output.
content.worked: The price of imported coffee rises while prices of domestically produced goods are unchanged. Coffee is in the consumer basket, so the increase can raise CPI. Because the coffee was produced abroad, it is not part of domestic GDP and does not directly raise the GDP deflator.

title: Indexing and Real Values

content.outcome: Convert nominal values across time and apply indexation.
content.core: A price index converts nominal amounts across time and can be used to index wages, benefits, rents, or tax thresholds. Converting an earlier nominal amount into later dollars requires multiplying by the later index divided by the earlier index. Indexation preserves purchasing power only when the chosen index and adjustment timing closely match the prices relevant to the recipient.
recognition: Identify the nominal amount, the starting index, and the ending index.
Scale the nominal amount by the ratio of the ending index to the starting index.
Check whether the contract uses the same index and adjustment timing as the prices relevant to the recipient.
A fully indexed nominal payment preserves purchasing power only to the extent that the index matches actual costs.
content.watch: Do not assume an indexed contract guarantees an exact real outcome in every circumstance. Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.
content.worked: A salary was $40,000 when CPI was 100. CPI is now 160. 40,000 x 160/100 = 64,000. Therefore, $64,000. Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.

title: Real versus Nominal Interest Rates

content.outcome: Calculate and interpret real and nominal interest rates.
content.core: The real interest rate approximately equals the nominal interest rate minus inflation. The nominal rate states how many additional dollars a lender receives, while the real rate measures the change in purchasing power. Expected inflation determines the ex ante real rate when a loan is made; actual inflation determines the ex post real return and can redistribute purchasing power between borrowers and lenders.
recognition: Unexpected inflation is higher than lenders and borrowers expected on a fixed-rate loan.
Actual inflation is lower than expected on a fixed nominal loan.
Unexpected inflation rises on a fixed-rate loan.
Actual inflation exceeds expected inflation while a loan’s nominal rate is fixed.
Ex ante real interest uses expected inflation; ex post real interest uses actual inflation.
content.watch: Do not use actual inflation to describe an expected return or expected inflation to describe the realized return. Ex ante real interest uses expected inflation; ex post real interest uses actual inflation.
content.worked: Nominal interest is 9% and inflation is 5%. Using the usual approximation, real interest is 9% - 5% = 4%. The exact real return is (1.09 / 1.05 - 1) x 100 = 3.81%. Higher-than-expected inflation lowers the realized real repayment burden and shifts purchasing power from lender to borrower.
content.check: What does a real interest rate describe that a nominal rate does not?

title: Living Standards and Growth

content.outcome: Use real GDP per person and compounding to compare living standards.
content.core: Real GDP per person is a common measure of material living standards, and compounding makes sustained growth powerful over time. Dividing real output by population distinguishes growth in total production from growth in average material resources. Productivity growth can raise output per person without requiring proportionally more work, although this measure does not capture every dimension of well-being.
recognition: A country raises output mainly by requiring much longer workweeks, while output per hour is unchanged.
Higher productivity lets an economy produce more goods and services from its available labor and resources.
Real GDP per person is commonly used to compare living standards and growth.
Real GDP per person relates inflation-adjusted output to the number of people sharing that output.
Compare growth in real GDP with population growth to distinguish total output from output per person.
content.watch: A common mistake is to equate more total labor input with higher productivity or complete welfare improvement. Productivity is output per unit of input, and GDP omits important dimensions of well-being.
content.worked: If real GDP per person grows at 4% per year, the Rule of 70 estimates a doubling time of 70/4 = 17.5 years. This calculation describes material output growth, not complete well-being: longer work hours can raise GDP per person without raising output per hour or preserving leisure.
content.check: At 4% annual growth, about how many years does the Rule of 70 predict for real GDP per person to double?

title: Productivity Measurement

content.outcome: Calculate output per worker and interpret productivity changes.
content.core: Labor productivity measures output per worker or per hour worked. For example, 2,400 units produced in 300 labor hours means 2,400 / 300 = 8 units per hour. Productivity compares output with the labor input used to produce it, so changes in both output and labor matter. A country can consume more when its workers produce more output per worker.
recognition: Measure labor productivity as real output per worker or per hour worked.
Compare output using the same amount of labor when evaluating a productivity change.
An increase in total output is not necessarily a productivity increase if labor input also rises.
On a production-function graph, diminishing returns make equal additions of capital add progressively less output.
content.watch: Do not confuse total output with output per unit of labor. Productivity compares output with the labor input used to produce it, so changes in both output and labor matter.
content.worked: The graph shows output per worker of 28.53 when capital per worker is 20 and 36.37 when capital per worker is 40. The increase in labor productivity is 36.37 - 28.53 = 7.84 units per worker. Productivity measures output relative to labor input, not total output alone.
content.check: A business uses more labor hours but produces the same amount of output. What happens to labor productivity?

title: Sources of Productivity

content.outcome: Analyze physical capital, human capital, natural resources, and technology.
content.core: Productivity rises with physical capital, human capital, natural resources, and technological knowledge. Capital can have high returns where it is scarce. More capital per worker can raise output per worker, but the production function becomes flatter as capital deepens. Productivity compares output with the labor input used to produce it, so changes in both output and labor matter.
recognition: A worker receives a new machine that raises output with the same labor time.
More capital per worker can raise output per worker, but the production function becomes flatter as capital deepens.
The graph is upward sloping but becomes flatter as capital per worker rises.
A low-capital country buys machinery, but workers lack training and firms cannot reliably obtain electricity.
content.watch: Do not treat every increase in capital as producing the same output gain. More capital per worker can raise output per worker, but the production function becomes flatter as capital deepens.
content.worked: Increasing capital per worker from 20 to 40 raises output per worker from 28.53 to 36.37, a gain of 7.84. The production function becomes flatter as capital deepens, so equal additions to capital generate progressively smaller output gains. That curvature shows diminishing returns to capital.
content.check: How does a worker's machine differ from the worker's training as a source of productivity?

title: Economic Growth Policy

content.outcome: Evaluate policies affecting long-run productivity and growth.
content.core: Long-run growth policy raises productive capacity rather than current spending alone. Saving and reliable finance support capital formation; education builds human capital; research and competition can advance technology. Stable property rights and institutions make firms more willing to invest. Because physical capital faces diminishing returns, sustained growth usually depends on several of these channels working together.
recognition: The policy changes capital formation, human capital, technology, or institutions.
The question distinguishes productive capacity from a temporary demand increase.
Reliable finance and property rights affect whether saving becomes productive investment.
The proposed change can raise output per worker over time.
content.watch: Do not treat a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity. Long-run growth policy works through productivity, capital formation, human capital, technology, and institutions.
content.worked: Capital deepening from 20 to 40 units per worker raises output per worker from 28.53 to 36.37, a gain of 7.84. Because the curve flattens, capital accumulation alone faces diminishing returns. Sustained growth also requires human capital, technology, and institutions that raise productivity.
